utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I'm going to call on counsel for Mr. Miletic first to give us an update. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Today we would like to proceed with my assistant and co-counsel, Norm Sepenuk, to present the first part of our oral argument and discussion. Thank you. And of course, I'll proceed with the other parts that we discussed yesterday afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And may it please the Judges of this honourable Chamber. Unlike the prior submissions to Your Honours, I'm not going to be speaking this morning about any factual disputes at all. What I'm going to be making here is purely a legal argument, and for the purpose of my legal argument, I'm going to assume arguendo that all of the government witnesses in this case have told the complete truth. And now I'd like to commence the legal argument I will be making. Mr. Beara was charged by the Prosecution and convicted by the Trial Chamber of genocide. The genocide charge being that Mr. Beara was a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica by killing the men and boys there and forcibly removing from the area the women, young children, and elderly men. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Beara intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, which included the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves as part of the Bosnian Muslim national ethnical group. In finding Mr. Beara guilty of genocide, the Trial Chamber acquitted him of the forcible transfer charge. In view of this acquittal, our argument in a nutshell is that Mr. Beara must also be acquitted on the genocide charge, since he did not have the genocidal intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia as a part of the protected group. The balance of my argument is devoted to the proposition that only a combination of the convictions for the mass killings of the men and the forcible transfer of the women and children that permits a finding of Mr. Beara's genocidal intent. Our argument is strongly supported, we submit, by the case law of this Tribunal, particularly by the holding of the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber in the Krstic case, to which I now would like to turn. Some ten years ago, in November 2003, I stood before this Appeals Chamber as co-counsel for General Radislav Krstic. General Krstic had been convicted by the Trial Chamber of genocide, forcible transfer, and other crimes arising out of the mass killings in the Srebrenica area of the military-aged men and the forcible transfer from the area to Bosnian Muslim-held territory of some 25.000 women, children, and elderly men. Granted -- and in finding General Krstic guilty of genocide, the Trial Chamber stated as follows, and I'm quoting from paragraph 595 of the Trial Chamber's opinion. "Granted, only the men" -- this is what the Trial Chamber said. "Granted, only the men of military age were systematically massacred, but it is significant that these massacres occurred at a time when the forcible transfer of the rest of the Bosnian Muslim population was well under way. The Bosnian Serb forces could not have failed to know, by the time they decided to kill all the men, that this selective destruction of the group would have a lasting impact upon the entire group. The Bosnian Serb forces knew, by the time they decided to kill all the military-aged men, that the combination of those killings with the forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly would inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica." On the appeal from this conviction, I argued at that time that though General Krstic was clearly involved in organising the bussing operation that effectuated the transfer of the women and children, that this should not be considered as a factor in determining genocidal intent, as the Trial Chamber had held. Our argument at that time, largely based on an analysis of the legislative history of the Genocide Convention of 1948, was that displacement of the population to another area was not evidence of genocide and could not be legally considered as such. To the contrary, we argued that the transfer of the women, children, and elderly men to safe areas under Bosnian Muslim control show that General Krstic's intent was not the indiscriminate group killing of, say, the Nazi and the Rwanda genocides, but rather indicated an intent to spare the group from any further harm. Well, as this Trial Chamber knows, we lost that argument. And in rejecting our argument, the Appeals Chamber stated - and I'd like to quote from the Appeals Chamber's findings and this is in paragraphs 31 -- 30 and 31 and 33, and this is what the Appeals Chamber said in rejecting that -- our argument at the time: "The Defence argues that the VRS decision to transfer, rather than to kill, the women and children of Srebrenica in their custody undermines the finding of genocidal intent. This conduct, the Defence submits, is inconsistent with the indiscriminate approach that has characterized all previously -- or previously recognized instances of modern genocide. "The decision of Bosnian Serb forces" -- continuing now with what the Appeals Chamber said. "The decision by Bosnian Serb forces to transfer the women, children, and elderly within their area -- within their control to other areas of Muslim-controlled Bosnia could be consistent with the Defence argument. This evidence, however, is also susceptible of an alternative interpretation. As the Trial Chamber explained, forcible transfer could be an additional means by which to ensure the physical destruction of the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica. The transfer completed the removal of the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica, thereby eliminating even the residual possibility that the Muslim community in the area could reconstitute itself." And then finally, this quotation from the Appeals Chamber, paragraph 33: "The Trial Chamber - as the best assessor of the evidence presented at trial - was entitled to conclude that the evidence of the transfer supported its finding that some members of the VRS Main Staff intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. The fact that the forcible transfer does not constitute in and of itself a genocidal act does not preclude a Trial Chamber from relying on it as evidence of the intentions of members of the VRS Main Staff. The genocidal intent may be inferred, among other facts, from evidence of 'other culpable acts systematically directed against the same group.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you just tell us where in the appeal brief this argument is found? What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The -- it's found, Your Honours, in the part of the appeal brief which talked about the Trial Chamber erred when it misapplied the element of mens rea required for the crime of genocide in finding that Beara had specific genocidal intent to destroy the targeted group, the targeted group being the Bosnian Muslims. That's on page 7 -- 71, I believe. I think it's 71, Your Honours, of the brief. And it's ground 19. And also the fact that it was not the only -- what happened was it was not the only reasonable inference on the evidence that Mr. Beara had genocidal intent. More specifically, in paragraph 224 of the trial brief where it said: "It is respectfully submitted that the Defence in this case has presented an abundance of evidence to support its claim that actions taken in the enclave, particularly those against the male population, were not taken with the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica and Zepa, though that Beara possessed at any moment such intent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue to develop your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'd like to refer also to the partial dissenting opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen, as this Chamber knows, a very distinguished former member of this Chamber. And Judge Shahabuddeen in his partially dissenting opinion agreed with all the notions of genocide intent that the majority had mentioned. His partial dissent had to do with -- he thought General Krstic was guilty of genocide, whereas the majority found him guilty -- they reduced charge from being a principal perpetrator to being an aider and abettor. But on the fundamental notion of genocidal intent, both the majority and Judge Shahabuddeen were together on that. And I think because his language is so precise and so accurate that -- bear with me, please, while I quote it. On paragraph 35 of his opinion, and he said this: "Thus, standing alone, forcible transfer is not genocide. But in this case the transfer did not stand alone, and that indeed is the basis on which the Appeals Chamber rejected the Defence argument that it showed that there was no genocide. It was part - an integral part - of one single scheme to commit genocide, involving killings, forcible transfer, and destruction of homes. In particular, it showed that the intent with which the killings were done was indeed to destroy the Srebrenica part of the Bosnian Muslim group. In my view, the judgement of the Appeals Chamber has to be understood as affirming that, by taking on the role of chief executor of the policy of forcible transfer," and here Judge Shahabuddeen was referring to General Krstic who sort of organised the bussing operation, "by taking on the role as chief executor of the policy of forcible transfer - an inseparable element of genocide - the appellant shared the intent of the Main Staff to commit the crime of genocide." And then again, just briefly, paragraph 57 of Judge Shahabuddeen's opinion, where he said: "No doubt, mere displacement does not amount to genocide. But, in this case, there was more than mere displacement. The killings, together with a determined effort to capture others for killing, the forced transportation or exile of the remaining population, and the destruction of homes and places of worship, constituted a single operation which was executed with the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part within the meaning of the chapeau to paragraph 2 of Article 4 of the Statute." Continuing Judge Shahabuddeen, just one more -- two more sentences: "It was this combination of factors to which the Trial Chamber referred when it stated in paragraph 595 of its judgement that the 'Bosnian Serb forces knew, by the time they decided to kill all the military-aged men, that the combination of these killings with the forcible transfer of the women, children, and elderly would inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica.'" I believe it's fair to say that the Krstic appeals judgement has become the leading and most authoritative case on the subject of genocide, and particularly as to any alleged genocidal conduct that occurred in the Srebrenica area at the times in question. Following the Krstic appeals judgement, all of the Srebrenica cases have involved indictments charging a combination of the killings and the forcible transfer from Srebrenica. These include the Blagojevic and Jokic cases and also they include the Tolimir, Karadzic, and Mladic cases. The template for these latter cases was set by the Krstic appeal judgement. In each of the subsequent cases, in each of these cases, the Prosecution has followed the holding and rationale of the Krstic appeal judgement by indictments which charge the commission of genocide by a combination of the mass killings of the military-aged men and the forcible transfer of the women and children, resulting in the destruction of the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. For example, in the Tolimir trial judgement, involving essentially the same set of facts of mass murder and forcible transfer in Srebrenica, the Trial Chamber held at paragraph 1157: "... the protected group - the Bosnian Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia - was murdered and suffered serious bodily and mental harm by acts of murder and forced movement, and that the conditions resulting from the acts of Bosnian Serb Forces as part of the combined effect of the forcible removal and murder operations, were deliberately inflicted and calculated to lead to the physical destruction of the Bosnian Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia." Which brings me now to a discussion of the present case involving Mr. Beara. What I call the Krstic appeal judgement template was used in this case, in the case involving Mr. Beara, involving, as it did, the charging of genocide by the Prosecution which combined the mass murders of the men with the forcible transfer of the women and children. And before turning to the indictment itself, we first note that the Prosecution successfully moved for the joinder of Mr. Beara's case with the other co-defendants and alleged as follows, and I quote: "All the indictments relate to the same transaction, a common scheme whose purpose was to ethnically cleanse the Eastern Bosnian enclaves. Specifically, the scheme consisted of two interrelated joint criminal enterprises. One to 'force the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves' and the second 'to murder all the able-bodied men captured from the Srebrenica enclave.'" That's in paragraph 9 of the motion. And now, turning to the indictment itself in Mr. Beara's case, the indictment alleges that Pandurevic, Beara, Popovic, Nikolic, and Borovcanin committed genocide, and I'm looking at paragraph 26 now of the indictment: "With the intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim people as a national ethnical or religious group. "(A) kill members of the group by summary execution, including both planned and opportunistic summary executions, as described in this indictment; "(B) cause serious bodily or mental harm to both female and male members of the Bosnian Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa, including, but not limited to, the separation of able-bodied men from their families and the forced movement of the population from their homes to areas outside the RS." And the indictment further alleged in paragraph 33 as follows: "The forcible transfer of women and children from Srebrenica and Zepa, as described in this indictment, created conditions known to the accused that would contribute to the destruction of the entire Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia, including, but not limited to, the failure of the population to live and reproduce normally." Based on this indictment alleging a combination of murder and forcible transfer as acts of genocide, the Trial Chamber summarised the theory of the Prosecution's case as follows, this is in paragraph 838 of the Trial Chamber's opinion, and I quote: "The Prosecution alleges that a decision was taken to destroy the Bosnian Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia, which was implemented primarily by separating, forcibly transferring, and ultimately killing members of the group." Thus, the Prosecution, based presumably on the Krstic appeal judgement holding, determined that the genocide conviction of Mr. Beara required genocidal intent with respect to both the execution of the men and the forcible transfer of the women and children. Now, the Trial Chamber acquitted Mr. Beara on the forcible transfer charge, and here's what the Trial Chamber said in paragraph 1334 of the opinion: "The Trial Chamber has found that while Beara knew of the common plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population, he did not make a significant contribution to it. Similarly, the evidence is insufficient to establish that he aided and abetted forcible transfer in either Srebrenica or Zepa, nor does it demonstrate that he is responsible for forcible transfer through another mode of liability. The Trial Chamber therefore finds that Beara is not criminally responsible for forcible transfer as a crime against humanity." In view of Colonel Beara's acquittal on the forcible transfer charge, our argument is that he must also be acquitted of genocide. This is so because the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber, in following the holding and rationale of the Krstic appeal judgement, determined that the relevant group was the Bosnian Muslims, that is, some 1.400.000 people, the relevant group was the Bosnian Muslims, and that the part of the group targeted for destruction were the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, including the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, approximately 40.000 people comprising some 2.9 per cent of the Bosnian Muslim population. This was considered by both the Trial and Appeals Chambers in the Krstic case to be a sufficiently substantial number to meet the requirements of the law of genocide, particularly since the murders and forcible transfer operation essentially resulted in the annihilation of the Bosnian Muslim group in Eastern Bosnia, as both the Trial and Appeals Chamber held. By acquitting Colonel Beara on the forcible transfer charge, the only genocidal conduct for which Mr. Beara could be held accountable is the murder of an estimated 5300 men, which is the figure used by the Trial Chamber in this case. Horrible as such killings, indeed any killings, are, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber have not claimed that the killings of the men which comprise less than one half of 1 per cent of the Bosnian Muslim population, meets the substantiality requirement of the law of genocide or constitutes a legally significant part of the targeted group. This being so, how did the Trial Chamber arrive at its finding that Colonel Beara -- that Mr. Beara was guilty of genocide? Here's what the Trial Chamber held, paragraphs 861, 862, and 863 of the opinion: "The Trial Chamber finds that the murder operation - from the separations to detention to execution and burial - was a carefully orchestrated strategy to destroy aimed at the Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia. As found earlier, through this murderous enterprise, the underlying acts of killing and the infliction of serious bodily and mental harm were committed. The Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond all reasonable doubt that these acts were perpetrated with genocidal intent. The Trial Chamber" -- the Trial Chamber is going on, paragraph 862: "The Trial Chamber draws further support for its conclusion from 'the other culpable acts systematically directed against the same group' in the same time-period, notably the forcible transfer operation and its accompanying circumstances aimed at the population in Potocari. The frenzied efforts to forcibly remove the remainder of the population, while the male members of the community were targeted for murder, provides further evidence that the intent was to destroy." Finally in paragraph 863, and I quote: "Thus the Trial Chamber is satisfied that genocide was committed by members of the Bosnian Serb Forces, including members of the VRS Main Staff, the VRS Security Branch, such as Popovic and Beara, against the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, as part of the Bosnian Muslims." So clearly, the Trial Chamber, by also mentioning the forcible transfer along with the murders, recognised that this -- it was this combination of factors that resulted in a finding that Mr. Beara had the genocidal intent to destroy the Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia. However, the Trial Chamber acquitted Colonel Beara of the forcible transfer charge with respect to the removal of the Bosnian Muslim population from both Srebrenica and Zepa, nor was the evidence found sufficient by the Trial Chamber to even sustain an aiding and abetting charge as to either enclave on the forcible transfer issue. What the Trial Chamber did find was: "... that while Beara knew of the common plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population, he did not make a significant contribution to it." And therefore acquitted him of the forcible transfer charge. Our respectful submission is that it is not enough in finding genocidal intent to justify Colonel Beara's genocide conviction because he allegedly knew of the plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population. The special intent requirement of the law of genocide, the dolus specialis, if you will, that we associate with genocide, the crime of crimes, surely required the Prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Colonel Beara had the specific intent not only to murder the men but to forcibly transfer the women, children, and elderly men from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sepenuk, but are you saying that the genocidal intent can't be inferred from the killings on their own?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm saying, Your Honour, yes. That it cannot. That you need a combination of the killings and the forcible transfer, because if it was just the killings of the men, I don't think that would show the intent to destroy the entire Bosnian Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia. That's the requirement of the Krstic appeal judgement, that the -- that the definition of genocide under those circumstances is to annihilate, to eliminate, the whole Srebrenica/Zepa enclave and the people therein. It doesn't have to do with just the -- if it was just the men, that wouldn't destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, that would just be the military-aged men. I don't think it's substantial either -- number one, it doesn't meet the test of substantiality; and number two, it would violate the -- what the Krstic decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying 5.300 would not meet the test of substantiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. And, you know, Your Honour, it's a difficult argument to make in terms of -- speaking now flatly as a humanitarian or as a member of the human race, but I am saying that, yes, one-half of 1 per cent I don't think meets the substantiality requirement. But more specifically, it doesn't show the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, which was the -- what the Krstic appeal judgement required and presumably what the Trial Chamber in this case required. It was -- you know, there was no idea that it was just the men as opposed to the Srebrenica enclave. It was destruction of the Srebrenica enclave, and I'm saying: Yes, it's not enough just to show the murders of the men, horrific and horrible and terrible as that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What's that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. The genocidal intent required by the Krstic Appeals Chamber imposed on the Prosecution the duty to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Beara intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia by a combination of the mass killings of the men and the forcible transfer of the women and children. By his acquittal on the forcible transfer charge, the Prosecution has not proved the requisite genocidal intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. Therefore, Colonel Beara should be acquitted of the genocide, at the least. As required by the well-established rule of this Appeals Chamber, a finding of genocide is not the only reasonable conclusion to be derived from the evidence in this case. Unless there are any questions, that's the conclusion of my argument, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An interesting argument. We'll, no doubt, hear from Mr. Rogers on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in my overview, I shared with you the first part that Mr. Sepenuk was going to proceed and argue. And also, I told you that we were going to address the Trial Chamber's errors, both legally and factually, as it relates to their findings with respect to Mr. Beara, regarding the joint criminal enterprise to commit murder as well as their finding with respect to the genocidal intent that purportedly he had. In doing so, the Trial Chamber utilised certain evidence which, as we stated yesterday, was unreliable, untrustworthy, and not corroborated. But before we go into the detail, as I highlighted several individuals, the Court and every court, I believe, has to look at these outside or extraneous factors. They look principally for three things: To make a determination if an individual was a participant in a JCE to commit murder in this case, and whether he significantly contributed to it, and then they also look at those same factors for genocidal intent. Those three factors, I think, is somewhat highlighted by the Trial Chamber, although erroneously applied, were the words, were the physical presence, as well as the actions. It's incredibly and, most respectfully, important, I believe, that we properly distinguish each of those three: The words, physical presence, and actions. The Prosecution, unfortunately, mixes those three, simply in an attempt to cloud the issues. I think not only should we distinguish each three, but we should also make a further distinction as to each day as it relates to Mr. Beara. The Trial Chamber noted on paragraph 1299 that there was no direct evidence before it of Mr. Beara's participation in the murder operation prior to July 13th. It's not appeal, it's a fact that we accept and are living with. But the implicit is that there is indirect evidence of his participation in the murder operation. Before we address that, we should examine when on July 13th was Mr. Beara allegedly a participant in this joint criminal enterprise. We suggest, based on the trial record and what the Trial Chamber found, it couldn't have been before his purported 8.00 meeting with Mr. Deronjic. The Deronjic evidence is highly suspect for numerous reasons, as I've tried to outline yesterday. That is the only individual who claims that Mr. Beara spoke to him and used the words "kill all." It is the basis of that conversation, those words, that the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Beara was a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber seemingly relies on other evidence to establish corroboration, but they mix the elements. Who else was present with Mr. Beara when he allegedly used those words "kill all" the Bosnian Muslims? No one. Dissecting the trial record as often as you'd like, the only conclusion that a reasonable Trial Chamber could have found was that that evidence was not corroborated. In fact, the Trial Chamber in analysing whether they were going to admit the evidence pursuant to 92 quater of Miroslav Deronjic on the 21st of April, 2008, stated as follows, and I quote: "Deronjic's testimony includes evidence pertaining to proof of acts and conduct of the Accused Pandurevic, Borovcanin, and Beara, including the whereabouts of Pandurevic and Borovcanin in July 1995 and Beara's alleged visit to and conversation with Deronjic in his office in Bratunac in the evening of 13 July 1995." And that was on paragraph 58. It proceeds in determining whether it should admit this evidence to state the following: "The Trial Chamber acknowledges that Deronjic's evidence," one, "contains a number of inconsistencies"; two, has "admissions of prior false statements"; and three, "includes uncorroborated claims." Interestingly, it makes the following observation: "This is not disputed by the Prosecution." The Trial Chamber at that point knew that the Prosecution acknowledged and did not dispute the lack of credibility and reliability of the Deronjic evidence; however, in that decision perhaps the most gleaning thing we can see is found on paragraph 62, page 15, where the Trial Chamber states: "What is uncorroborated is his evidence as to the specifics of the meeting and conversation between him and Beara on 13 July." Again, it's paragraph 62, page 15 of their April 21st, 2008, decision. The Prosecution has generally stated, even yesterday, we have to look at the quantity of the evidence. I suggest we look at both, the quality and the quantity of the evidence. The quantity alone may establish certain issues with respect to physical presence or certain issues with respect to action, but there is no evidence to corroborate Deronjic's claim that Beara was in his office and Deronjic's claim that Beara used the words "kill all." The Trial Chamber erred when it accepted that evidence. The Trial Chamber below erred because it mixed the three fundamental elements and confused the issues of words, physical presence, and actions. These issues, as the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1215 of its decision stated, and they claimed, respectfully, that they were going to exercise caution in assessing and attributing any weight to the Deronjic evidence. And they stated that they: "Looked for corroboration with reference to those parts that relates to critical issues ..." At 1215, they tell us they're going to look to find corroborating evidence to those parts that relates to critical issues. What more critical issue can we have when a man is indicted and charged with genocide and other crimes against humanity and the basis of that charge and allegation is that he told someone purportedly, while they were drunk, late at night, with no one else being present: Kill all? Respectfully, the Trial Chamber grossly erred and should not at the first instance admitted the evidence of Mr. Deronjic, but no reasonable Trial Chamber would have given any weight to Deronjic's testimony as it relates to Mr. Beara and that conversation. Let me briefly highlight for you where the Trial Chamber used that evidence of Deronjic, to show you that the impact it had poisoned and infected the entire trial judgement as it related to Mr. Beara. With respect to the JCE to murder, I invite you to look at the two paragraphs of 1301 and 1302, where the Trial Chamber states, in connection with

utterances.speaker: MR. BEARA
utterances.text: "... his contribution to the common purpose cannot be classified as anything other than significant and by his actions," separate element, "and words there can be no doubt that he," Beara, "shared the intent to murder on a massive scale." All three in my view - actions, words, and physical presence - in some instances need to be present. The Trial Chamber found that the actions and words -- what words? It goes on to say, and in order to determine what words the Trial Chamber relied on when it stated this in paragraphs 1301 and 1302, we simply have to look to the preceding paragraph, 1300. At paragraph 1300, the Trial Chamber therein references the only words and they state as follows: "The first evidenced act on the part of Beara illustrates well the pivotal and high level role he played in the murder operation. He arrives on 13 July at the offices of the President of the Bratunac SDS with an order 'from the top' to kill all the Bosnian Muslim males housed in and around Bratunac." If the Trial Chamber properly excluded the unreliable evidence of Deronjic and if it properly excluded this uncorroborative evidence, it would not have concluded that Beara was either a member of the joint criminal enterprise to murder and most certainly it would not have concluded that Ljubisa Beara significantly contributed to the joint criminal enterprise to murder. There certainly is and exists other evidence other than Deronjic as it relates to Mr. Beara, but with respect to those words, the Trial Chamber relied solely and exclusively, in our opinion, or at the very least predominantly on the evidence of Deronjic. The Deronjic evidence has previously found to be notoriously uncorroborated statements, grave inconsistencies in his testimony, his status as a war criminal, benefitting from a plea agreement, the sole nature of his evidence against Beara relates to the acts and conduct of Beara. Interestingly another Trial Chamber in this courthouse, namely, the Karadzic case, had a similar issue, where the Deronjic evidence was offered by the Prosecution, despite the fact - and this is a public record - despite the fact that the Prosecution knew and knows that it's grossly unreliable and should be given no weight. The Trial Chamber in that case rejected the Prosecution's application to admit such evidence. Curiously, the Trial Chamber in its decision, however, knowing of the decision of the Trial Chamber in this case, they tried to distinguish the case and merely distinguished it by stating that in the Karadzic case Deronjic's testimony went to more inordinate acts. There is no recognised standard that one act or more than one act should or should not be the test or the degree to accept or exclude evidence. The rule and jurisprudence is to look whether or not that evidence is credible, whether it's reliable; and if reliable, not just relevant, but if reliable, then you can determine to assess the weight to be given. Given the law in this jurisprudence that there was no corroboration of that very evidence, that Mr. Deronjic and the Trial Chamber relied upon, we believe that it should be excluded and that the case should be reviewed without the evidence of Mr. Deronjic. It simply invalidates the Trial Chamber's convictions of Mr. Beara. The Trial Chamber doesn't stop, though, to use the Beara evidence -- I mean the Deronjic evidence against Mr. Beara just for joint criminal enterprise, as I said. It relies on it extensively to establish special intent in genocide. It even goes further and relies on it in its sentencing of Mr. Beara. I invite you to look with respect to the genocide issue at the Trial Chamber's decision paragraph 1314. This is what they say and I'm highlighting some of it for you: "... his grim determination to kill as many as possible as quickly as possible. His encounters with Deronjic on the night of 13 July provide a chilling illustration of a mind set on destruction. He," Beara, "announces an intent to 'kill all' the detained men, and without pause to consider or comment upon the horrific nature of his 'orders' he launches into a series of heated exchanges about the best location for this reprehensible undertaking." The Trial Chamber also says, as I stated earlier, at paragraph 1311: "There is no direct ... evidence that Beara had the requisite specific intent for genocide ..." But what they're looking at are the words purportedly stated by Mr. Beara and rely heavily, as I've just highlighted on paragraph 1314, the words that only one individual who was convicted, who lied on multiple occasions in court, who changed his story multiple times, the Trial Chamber relied on that evidence. We continue to object and we believe that that evidence should be given no weight in the consideration and should be excluded. When we -- the Trial Chamber then also goes on and talks about: Well, other people saw Beara at Bratunac SDS. It's interesting that the people the Trial Chamber suggests are reliable and credible to confirm his physical presence were Mr. Borovcanin, Mr. Simic, PW-161, and PW-170. Well, we know Mr. Borovcanin, he did not testify in this case. His interview with the Prosecution was admitted, again subject to 92 quater. Again, does Mr. Beara have any rights? Should he not be presumed innocent? Should he at the least not have the right to cross-examine the witnesses which make any allegations as it relates to him? Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber, we believe, erred because it used Borovcanin's statement to confirm what Deronjic stated. Borovcanin was not present when the discussion between -- allegedly between Beara and Deronjic occurred. Borovcanin does not say that he overheard Beara ever using the word "kill all." The Trial Chamber just says that they were present and Borovcanin allegedly saw them together arguing. Similarly, the Trial Chamber relies heavily on another individual with, I think, less credibility, if possible, than Deronjic, and that is Momir Nikolic, another individual who is notorious for his inconsistent statements, notorious for giving false statements, notorious for changing his own plea agreements to benefit himself, and ultimately he claims, without having any corroboration, that Beara at some point used words to kill or destroy the Bosnian males in Bratunac. His evidence, likewise, although admitted, should be given no weight whatsoever. Again, why? It goes to critical issues of acts and conduct of Mr. Beara and it is not corroborated. We're not seeking, as the Prosecution, to say the quantitative evidence corroborates it. We're dissecting it and saying: At that instance, was that conversation corroborated by any individual who has at least some trustworthiness, some credibility, some reliability? I submit to you that the Trial Chamber erred when it utilised the evidence of Borovcanin, Momir Nikolic, and Deronjic in assessing Beara's words and his physical presence on July 13th, 1995. No other evidence exists with respect to Mr. Beara about July 13th, 1995. He comes to the scene late, he comes to the scene at night supposedly, and he walks around aimlessly throughout the town of Bratunac by himself. One witness the Court purportedly relies upon is a gentleman by the name of Simic, Ljubisa or Ljubomir Simic. And you can see in footnote 4118 of the trial transcript [sic], he states that someone told him that Ljubisa Beara was in the offices of the SDS. And he goes on to say he was told later that it was probably Beara. Deronjic's testimony, as unreliable as it is, he suggests that Simic was asleep so he wouldn't know. We can't allow this purported corroborating testimony even for the presence, the physical presence, of an accused or an individual when it's solely given by unreliable and untrustworthy witnesses. The Court also relies on PW-170, and that's on paragraph 1268. It's glaring what the Court says about that Witness PW-170. In fact, it concedes that PW-170 does not indicate Beara was at the meeting, but it's using it as corroborating evidence. The logic utilised by the Trial Chamber failed in many respects. It failed because I think the end result was looked at respectfully and I think that they adopted, unfortunately, the theory and themes of the Prosecution that quantity is more important than quality. We discussed briefly yesterday physical presence, we're turning to 14th July, the evidence as to where Mr. Beara and his whereabouts on the 14th July. Egbers, one of the witnesses that was called and testified, and I invited my colleague to give him the cites on it. Mr. Egbers, I stated, was supposedly at a meeting where he was introduced to Mr. Beara and in that meeting was an individual by the name of Zoran Malinic. And the Chamber invited me to give you some cites in the record. If we look at just the Trial Chamber's judgement, paragraph 1220, as well as paragraph 1260 specifically states that Zoran Malinic and an interpreter were present during this encounter purportedly with Mr. Beara and Egbers. Likewise, the opening statement of the OTP on the 21st of August, 2006, they clearly start on page 41 -- or 411, lines 24 through 25, and continuing on the next page, 415 -- 412, I'm sorry, 412, lines 1 through 5, that the OTP suggests that on or about July 13/14, although it's confirmed now it was the 14th, DutchBat Lieutenant-Colonel or soldier Vincent Egbers was in Nova Kasaba and the commander Malinic - although they misspelled it in the transcript, they have it Malonic, but I don't believe we have a dispute on that - introduce Beara: Here is my commander. Further to the evidence that this conversation was not simply one-on-one was the transcript of the testimony of Vincent Egbers on the 19th of October, 2006, where he clearly states that he was with Zoran Malinic at Nova Kasaba for two days, like -- and that was on page 2818 and also on page 2855, the following day, October 20th. This is what Egbers says: "... I'd never ever heard of Colonel Beara, his existence" -- THE APPELLANT POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. THE APPELLANT POPOVIC: [Interpretation] I must use the toilet, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's five past. We'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the immediate break I was just going to conclude the evidence with respect to Mr. Egbers and my comments yesterday. Egbers, on October 20th, 2006, in his testimony on page 2855, lines 17 through 22, he states he's never heard of Beara. He's never heard of his existence. And he was there with the interpreter and Zoran Malinic and they told him about Colonel Beara. The point of all this is the Prosecution makes a lot of claims with respect to Mr. Beara's presence in or around the area of Bratunac and Zvornik. So his presence is important. But present or not, you can still have culpability in a crime. Obviously we understand just peripherally that Karadzic wasn't in Bratunac or Zvornik and he's charged with similar crimes. So presence is important but not as important as the Prosecution would like us to believe. Nevertheless, when they allege and assert that that presence is an indicator or a great factor that should be applied, they're required under the law, under the jurisprudence in this court, to corroborate that evidence. I suggested yesterday that the burden of proof clearly falls on them with respect to Mr. Egbers and whether or not Beara was at Nova Kasaba on the 14th of July, 1995. They had access to and were responsible and were duty-bound to present corroborating evidence. If Mr. Beara was there, why didn't the Prosecution call Zoran Malinic? If Beara was at Nova Kasaba on the 14th of July, why didn't they call Egbers' own interpreter? If Ljubisa Beara was really there on the 14th of July, 1995, why didn't they call any other DutchBat who was with Mr. Egbers? There were at least six or eight of them. Each one of those individuals surely would have remembered Mr. Beara or could have given testimony. The inference, I believe, that the Trial Chamber erred in making is that Mr. Beara was not there. The Trial Chamber should have inferred with uncorroborated testimony that Mr. Beara was not present at Nova Kasaba on the 14th of July, 1995. Interestingly, I think if we look at a dissenting opinion in Tolimir case, which is a public record, Mr. Egbers' credibility is questioned, rightfully so. His demeanour was questioned at that trial, his recollection was questioned. One honourable Judge in another case suggested that Mr. Egbers' testimony should also be given no weight and gave it no weight just like she gave no weight to Momir Nikolic and/or other individuals and accused who gave testimony in that case. I suggest the same be done here. Accepting Egbers' view, accepting Egbers' testimony was erroneous. It invalidates the judgement as it relates to Mr. Beara so far as physical presence, of him being present, is considered as being a significant factor. I'm only highlighting some of the evidence. Certainly other people -- and we've questioned their identification of Beara, but to move on to the next day, the 15th of July, 1995, the Trial Chamber again uniquely, unseen, in my view, respectfully, in other cases, it utilises and examines the testimony of a Witness PW-165. That can be found in the trial judgement at 1227 and 1228. The claim with respect to PW-165 was Beara's presence with Popovic at the Standard barracks purportedly at 6.30 p.m. on July 15th. I don't know if you've read it and just indulge me so I can just share it. The trial record in analysing that evidence found that this PW-165 did indeed identify another accused in this case, but it states as it relates to Mr. Beara at 1228: "The Trial Chamber has previously found that PW-165's subsequent identification of Popovic as one of the men that he saw, combined with the evidence of what he was told, was sufficient to satisfy the Trial Chamber that Popovic was present ..." It goes on to say: "This is not the same in the case of Beara, as PW-165 did not see him at the time other than from the back and he was not able to subsequently identify him, thus PW-165 does not directly identify Beara as having been present ..." So far we're probably all respectfully in agreement with that. The Trial Chamber unfortunately and regrettably went further and erred as it found on that same paragraph. "However, the fact remains that PW-165 was told that this was Beara and Popovic, and that information was confirmed in part by the subsequent identification of Popovic ..." We're talking about in this paragraph Beara's identification, but the Trial Chamber's convinced that Popovic is there, right or wrong. But they're utilising the identification of Popovic to try to suggest that that means that Beara was there even though this gentleman did not see Beara at all and the Trial Chamber recognises that. They go on further and their reasoning is what we're questioning and what we've appealed here: "When considered in combination with other evidence, especially as to Beara's presence in the area at the time, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that Beara was present with Popovic at the Standard Barracks in the early evening of 15 July 1995." They're satisfied? Did they meet what's required, that there was no reasonable doubt that Beara was there? If it's as critical as the Prosecution has stated it was and has indicated as it is, his physical presence at all these sites, the Trial Chamber says it's true, he didn't identify Beara; but because he identified Popovic, it's good enough for now. No corroboration, no explanation that I respectfully believe is reasoned with respect to this and other witnesses. All this goes to the Court's -- Trial Chamber's finding of special intent. At paragraph 1318 of its trial judgement, it highlights certain factors that it considered and considered to be decisive in finding that Ljubisa Beara had special intent. 1318, they rely on his words, words that he create -- or words that Mr. Beara purportedly made to whom, the Deronjic evidence, the unreliable, uncorroborated evidence, his demonstrated determination to kill as many as possible. That's the same quote they used when they cited and relied on solely the Deronjic evidence, pursuant to his instructions, as if Mr. Beara was giving instructions to Deronjic, again relying on the Deronjic evidence. It does list other acts, it does state that you look at the scale and scope of the killing operation that was carried out with his knowledge, but I suggest to you that if he was not present and he did not utilise those words, what evidence would there be as it relates to Ljubisa Beara? Scant at best. The Trial Chamber erred and failed to distinguish between words, physical presence, and actions, and instead they took the approach of quantitative instead of qualitative evidence. I suggest, respectfully, that in analysing Mr. Ljubisa Beara, that we carefully scrutinise each and every instance when his conduct or his actions may lead to a conviction. That is the only way that Mr. Beara can be afforded a guarantee of a fair trial. I respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber erred and the judgement should be invalidated. If I may now turn in the interest of time to the question this Chamber has asked me with respect to Jadar River and Trnovo. In our view, respectfully, the Trial Chamber did not properly assess and identify whether the physical perpetrators of the crimes committed were members of the JCE. There is jurisprudence that suggests that there must be a link, and I believe the link is necessary in order to convict an individual for crimes that were committed by others outside of the JCE. The Brdjanin Appeals Chamber suggests at pages -- at paragraphs 412 and 413: "The existence of this link is a matter to be assessed on a case-by-case basis." This was not done by the Trial Chamber below. However, it seems that this may be co-perpetration -- strike that. Nevertheless, the Court also looked at the Appellate Chamber's decision in Martic and held that the Trial Chamber failed to make an explicit finding in how members of the JCE used physical perpetrators, paragraph 181. Perpetrators in those cases were identified as having been used as tools, tools implying a high degree of control over those perpetrators who committed those crimes. I believe the dissenting opinion by Judge Kwon addresses the Trnovo issue, but likewise, I think the issue with respect to Jadar River as well as other instances applied to Mr. Beara but it should not be -- a conviction should not be held on those. Finally another appeals judgement addresses the issue of linking and the necessary link and that is the Krajisnik appellate judgement. In Krajisnik, the Trial Chamber held that the establishment of a link between the crime and member of the JCE is a matter to be assessed on a case-by-case basis, at paragraph 235, and it reviewed the Trial Chamber's finding to determine whether this link was established and whether the perpetrators were used by the JCE members --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was hoping not to hear that. I've heard it. Thank you. I apologise. The Krajisnik Appeals Chamber did the right thing when they found that they lacked the necessary link and they quashed Krajisnik's convictions in relation to a number of crime scenes and crime sites. In the instant case with respect to the Appellate Chamber's question on Jadar River and Trnovo, we would like to expand it and suggest to the Trial Chamber, if we accept that Ljubisa Beara was present at 8.00 p.m. on July 13th in Bratunac, he joined purportedly the JCE that evening. There's no evidence, as the Court stated in its trial decision, of his direct participation prior to that. When did the Kravica murders happen? That day earlier. The conviction with respect to the Kravica murders should be quashed as well in our respectful submission. I hope I've answered the question raised by the Trial Chamber adequately enough. I'd like to turn, if I may, to just the next couple of sections of our oral submissions, and we yesterday mentioned it's a category that I've coined: Seeking the truth and exculpatory evidence. We lump it together because we believe that if we get to the truth, perhaps that truth will also be exculpatory to Mr. Beara. Indeed, I believe that it is. We'd like first to discuss, as we did orally yesterday, Exhibit P886, and I've given it, I think -- if we could put it on the ELMO so that everyone can see it. So we -- I'll just proceed and I think we can catch up. I invite this honourable Chamber to examine the evidence of the trial record P886. It's important to note the date of this exhibit, 13th July, when the purported murder or the murder operation indeed started and the killings started in Bratunac. Curiously, the drafter of this memo or note was the chief of the centre of Zvornik public security - it's up now - Dragomir Vasic. The contents are chilling, indeed. He states, Mr. Vasic, who's part of the Zvornik public sector security centre, totally different from Ljubisa Beara and others, he states that he had a meeting with Mladic that same day, 13th July 1995, and they were informed that the VRS was continuing operations towards Zepa, leaving all other work to the MUP as follows: 1, the evacuation process. 2 is the part that I believe is chilling. He states: "Killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje. Fighting is going on. This job is being done solely by the MUP units ..." solely by the MUP units. The Prosecution knows this witness. The Prosecution has identified him in their case, and this witness, I believe without any dispute, sat here for two and a half weeks and ultimately was withdrawn as a witness in the underlying trial. What consideration did the Trial Chamber give, if any, to Dragomir Vasic's report? Scant, if at all. It was not interested to see if this was credible, reliable. It did not look at this as exculpatory or truthful for some reason. Why not? It's an admission. The Trial Chamber desperately reached on many occasions to suggest that Ljubisa Beara's words in intercepts meant something other than their plain text, but here we have a document that plainly states, a document that this gentleman probably -- or this person, I should say, never would have imagined would be found or published. He clearly states: "MUP was solely responsible." And the MUP units were doing this job solely. He identifies what job; no need to speculate. The next document I would like to just share briefly with the Chamber is 1D374, and 1D374 is a document we discussed briefly yesterday and it's a report from the United Nations Sector Civil Affairs unit by a gentleman by the name of Edward Joseph who drafted it. He testified in our case here. I would just like to direct the Appellate Chamber's focus on the second page of that document. I'm not sure if it's up yet. Oh, thank you. I don't have it on mine. That's why I was waiting. Thank you. If the Court looks at the second page of that document, it states under paragraph number 1, subsection 3 there with the dash, it states: "Up to three thousand were killed on the way, mostly by mines and BSA engagements ..." It would seem at first blush to be distasteful to discuss the killings, but if we're discussing the truth, we're by no way minimising the heroic efforts of the Bosnian Muslims in trying to reach freedom or trying to get to their homeland or trying to save their lives. But this Trial Chamber is required to look at all the evidence. The Trial Court and the Prosecution don't consider this evidence at all. We questioned their military expert, Richard Butler, on this issue. His responses were rather unique. He identified a term called "legitimate combat engagements," and he said it's legal, it's justified, and it's acceptable. We asked him if he reviewed or considered this document in his analysis, he stated he did not. He didn't think there was a need to. When we talk about numbers in this case, if it's significant whether it's a thousand, which is a horrific number, much less 5.000 or greater, one is unacceptable. But if we're going to create history and if we're going to establish historically what had occurred, this document should at the very least be given some consideration. Dismiss it. That would be acceptable as long as it's a reasoned opinion. If this Court finds that there was no legitimate combat engagements and that no one had died during the attack on Srebrenica and that all the dead were a result of a murderous operation, so be it. But I suggest to this Appellate Chamber, that's not the case, that the evidence is clear, it's reliable, it's corroborated, and it shows that 3.000 were killed as a result of mines and legitimate combat engagements, as Butler suggested. I have Butler's page number, if necessary, to look at his testimony. I invite the Appellate Chamber to look at pages 20.244, that's 20244, as well as 20245, among other references. We discussed this exhibit specifically with him on page 20290 and 20291, where Butler acknowledges that this document was not considered at all by him or any other member of his investigative team. The Trial Chamber had spent some time in analysing the intercepts and what Mr. Beara had said. They also discussed the intercept that we thought was plain, should be accepted as reliable, and that is the Exhibit 7D2D64 [sic]. The Trial Chamber -- and I'm trying to just get -- we get that up for you. The Trial Chamber addresses that exhibit in its judgement, and surprisingly it finds that it's not reliable because they claim that Mr. Beara knew he was being listened to. So Mr. Beara would have supposedly - and I know it seems speculative and I suggest that it is nothing but speculation - would have put out this type of intercept in order to somehow minimise his involvement. However, they don't use that same logic when they use intercept evidence against Mr. Beara and when they read-in what certain words mean in an intercept. This Exhibit 7D2D64 clearly states and establishes what the intent and mind-set of Mr. Ljubisa Beara was on 13 July 1995. He had at all times and was at all times only interested in the prisoners getting safe passage to the Batkovici camp, where they at that time would have interviewed, as all POWs are. This exhibit, I believe, is credible, it was not, again, created. It was an intercept that the Prosecution, in their quantitative amount of evidence they provide, and it was a Croat intercept, a third party provided this intercept. This intercept was not considered at all by the Trial Chamber as to Mr. Beara's participation in a joint criminal enterprise or as to his specific intent for the crime of genocide. I suggest that the Trial Chamber erred when it failed to give the proper weight to this evidence, and therefore its judgement is simply wrong and should be invalidated. I would like to address now just briefly the issues with -- relating to sentencing. We suggest that the Trial Chamber failed as a matter of law to apply and reduce the sentence, after recognising and accepting certain mitigating factors as being established and being reasonable. We brought evidence in the Defence case of Mr. Beara's good character, decent family, his actions of how he helped people prior and during the war of 1992 through 1995. We brought people of different ethnic backgrounds, which established that he assisted not only Bosnian Muslims, not only Croats, but also the Jewish community in Croatia while he was there. The Court found that he did have good character; however, it also found that they should give only limited weight to that. I suggest the Trial Chamber was wrong in giving limited weight to his good character. Ljubisa Beara surrendered to this Tribunal, one of the first to surrender. During the time when he pled, he urged others who were indicted to come forward and they slowly did. In fact, within six months four other individuals came forward. The Trial Chamber recognised that his surrender was a mitigating factor, rightfully so, but again it gave it limited weight. I say the next mitigating factor with respect to Mr. Beara, it's his age. We suggest that he's an advanced age and again we say it most respectfully. The Court said that they'll give some minimal weight to it. We also suggested as a mitigating factor that the Trial Chamber should examine the OTP's inconsistent theories of culpability and modes of liability as it related to Mr. Beara. At the opening of the underlying trial in this case, we played a tape of the OTP's -- not just suggestion, but their comment that Ljubisa Beara was "an empty vessel." The Trial Chamber addresses that and it believes that it has no importance. We believe that it has great importance, not just in sentencing but in the underlying aspects of culpability for Mr. Beara. If this Prosecution and the same gentleman in one case claims that Mr. Beara was an empty vessel and was not directly involved in any of the crimes by virtue of implication of using those words, how could this Prosecution in another case claim that he has direct and whole responsibility for those heinous crimes that occurred? It is our respectful submission that if mitigating evidence exists and if it's recognised and accepted by the Trial Chamber, then the sentence should be, indeed must be, reduced. Mr. Beara received the harshest sentence available: Life. No amount was reduced because of mitigating circumstances. The Trial Chamber further abused its discretion and erred when it failed to grant proper weight to the mitigating evidence. It failed to give the adequate amount of weight necessary for all those and other factors. The Trial Chamber further erred in its aggravation analysis. Respectfully, it should have looked at conduct for aggravation prior to, ancillary, or subsequent to the crimes that were charged to determine if a person has aggravating factors that should require or result in a greater punishment. There was no evidence other than good, decent character of Mr. Beara prior to or afterwards. I could understand an aggravating factor of a person's conduct to be utilised in aggravation to increase a sentence if his prior or subsequent conduct was considered immoral, perhaps illegal, perhaps even criminal. In this case, the Trial Chamber utilised the same underlying conviction, the same underlying purported crimes committed by Mr. Beara, and said: That's the reason we're going to sentence him and we found that there's aggravation. I suggest that that should not and is not the law of this jurisprudence. Utilising the same crimes for aggravation is cumulative, it's unnecessary, and it's a violation of the decision authority of this Chamber. We'd overall suggest, Your Honours, that Mr. Beara was not present during the times alleged, but more importantly, we assert that the evidence when scrutinised carefully is not corroborated that he used words which would justify him being a member and/or significantly contributing to the joint enterprise of murder, and most definitely his words did not constitute a finding that he had special intent for the crime of genocide. The Trial Chamber, in essence, merely utilises the evidence that they found erroneously of discriminatory intent and essentially just utilises that evidence in the other counts that were alleged against Mr. Beara for discriminatory intent, for crimes against humanity, et cetera. We believe that if we scrutinise the record carefully and examine and find that there was no corroborating evidence, that a just verdict can be entered in favour of Mr. Beara, whatever that may be. But as it stands now with these errors, we believe that there has been a miscarriage of justice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. Mr. Gillett will be making the majority of the submissions in this case, my colleague who sits behind me. So we'll swap over and he can continue and begin those submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly. I know you will want to address Mr. Sepenuk's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear -- yes. Yes, Mr. Gillett will deal with all those issues raised by Mr. Sepenuk and also by my learned friend Mr. Ostojic, and I will deal with the question at the conclusion, but he is prepared to deal with all of those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may it please the Court. As mentioned, my name is Matthew Gillett, and I'll present the arguments in response to the bulk of Mr. Beara's submissions in his brief and that you've heard yesterday and today. Your Honours, in July 1995, the Bosnian Serb forces systematically murdered thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys from the Srebrenica enclave. The Chamber held that Ljubisa Beara was instrumental in the planning and implementation of this mass murder. He was rightly convicted for his crimes, including extermination and genocide, and he was sentenced to the only appropriate sentence: Life imprisonment. In his appeal, Beara challenges almost every finding against him. He claims he was not in the Bratunac and Zvornik areas on 13 and 14 July 1995, and you've just heard that from his counsel at transcript page 40, he's maintained that Beara was not present. As you'll hear, that is incorrect, and that's incorrect on the basis of a variety of sources of evidence, independent sources, intercepted conversations, documents, and witnesses from various backgrounds --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the purposes of interpretation into B/C/S. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. Your Honours, Mr. Beara claims that even if his alibi is false and he was in these areas, he did not participate in the murder operation. And then, failing that, he argues that even if he was involved, heavily implicated in the murder of thousands of men and boys, he should not have received a life sentence. Each and every one of his arguments is flawed and his appeal should be rejected in its entirety. Now, in my submissions, I'll first set out Beara's key activities, his involvement in the murder operation. In the second part, I'll address some of my learned friends' challenges to the reliability of the evidence that the Chamber considered in reaching its findings. And then in the third part, I'll address the arguments concerning the JCE liability, joint criminal enterprise liability, and his conviction for genocide. And I will address specifically the arguments you've heard this morning. Given the time constraints, we will not be able to address every single one of his arguments, but we maintain our position in the Prosecution response brief. At the outset, I have to clear up some misstatements and misconceptions that I've heard during the Defence arguments and that are present in its brief and in its reply. For example, at paragraph 341 of his brief, Beara argues: "The Chamber erred when it found that willing participation of the accused constitutes an aggravating factor ..." and he refers to paragraph 2154 of the judgement. He's repeated more or less the same argument today. If you actually look at paragraph 2154 of the judgement, you'll see the Chamber found the exact opposite. It said that his willing participation was not an aggravating factor because it had already been taken into account. So it's simply not a fair reading of the trial judgement that is being presented to you. Secondly, there is a clear misunderstanding of the law that has been presented to you, the law that applies at this Tribunal. You've heard the Defence claim that the witness Vincent Egbers, who is a Dutch Battalion officer, should not have been received without corroboration, and that's at transcript page 28. They've said that the Office of the Prosecutor had a duty to present corroboration for this witness. This is fundamentally incorrect. It's well-established jurisprudence that the testimony of a single witness - and Egbers did testify - on a material fact does not require corroboration. That's in the Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 65; Aleksovski, paragraph 62; and the Kayishema appeal judgement, paragraph 154. Beara's arguments about Egbers simply repeat his trial submissions. The Chamber took these into account and addressed them in detail. This is an area for the Trial Chamber's discretion to assess. Egbers was introduced to Beara by name, and in fact the day after the meeting, 15 July, he noted down that he had indeed met Colonel Beara the previous day. This is an entirely reasonable basis for the Chamber to rely on his evidence and the Defence fails to show any error therein. Third, the Defence has completely ignored the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that apply at this Tribunal. They've attempted to sneak the evidence of the driver, Milos Tomovic, in through the back door and they've attempted to get that on the record in yesterday's transcript at page 101. If the Defence wanted this evidence, they should have called him as a witness and let him be subjected to cross-examination, and then we could have evaluated the weight of his evidence. They chose not to do so. And he was on the Defence list, you can see that at transcript page 31967. The Defence is highly misleading in yesterday's transcript when it said that an OTP investigator said Beara was in Belgrade on 13 to 15 July. This is untrue and they know it. What you've got is a misstatement of a document that is not even in evidence being presented to you. It is simply not worth your time to consider this argument. It can be summarily dismissed - I'm not sure which category, it would probably fit every category for summary dismissal. Similarly, the Defence arguments referring to Malinic are a red herring. He didn't testify; that's the end of the story. It's not evidence. You've heard the Defence refer to document 1D374 just previously, this is a report, they said the Chamber did not consider this. Again, incorrect. Footnote 2256 clearly shows that the Chamber did consider this. The report is vague, has very general numbers, and if you actually look in detail, it's notable that it leaves, if you do the maths, 6.000 Bosnian Muslims unaccounted for. That's quite close to the number that were, in fact, murdered during this killing operation. So there's nothing inconsistent about this document with the findings and it's certainly not a document that would have any impact on the findings. Now, Your Honours, these are just simply some examples to emphasise that you are going to have to take the Defence arguments with a grain of salt. You're also going to have to address the fact that the Defence arguments concerning genocide that have been raised this morning are a radical departure from its written brief. They are simply not contained in there. In fact, the Defence brief argues the opposite. Today they've said the Trial Chamber diverged from the Krstic Appeals Chamber's findings. In their brief, if you look at paragraph 221, you'll see that they say the Trial Chamber erred because it simply followed the Krstic appeal judgement. Which way is it? These two arguments are not compatible. Now, Your Honours, I will address the arguments that have been made, but they are an ambush and we may need to request extra time later in this hearing, upon reviewing the transcript, to see whether all the arguments have been covered. With these caveats in mind, I'll now turn to address Mr. Beara's activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what do you mean by reviewing the transcript to see whether all the arguments have been covered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, we've heard these arguments for the first time this morning; they're not contained in the brief. So we would respectfully reserve the right to read the transcript at the end of today's hearing and check whether everything has been covered sufficiently because I am taken off guard and I am going to have to address these on the fly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you find that they have not been covered, what would be your next step?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would make an application, and it would be for Your Honours to determine whether or not there was a sufficient basis. But we will cross that bridge when we come to it. Your Honours, with these caveats in mind, I will now set out some of Beara's key movements and activities in the killing operation, and I'll use some slides to do so. On the monitor we see a map of this area, of Bratunac and Zvornik, and I'll just check that Your Honours can all see that map. I see the time, Mr. President and Your Honours, and if you'd like to break before I enter this next section of my submissions -- otherwise, I can continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break. The break is for one hour and 30 minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before I resume my submissions, I'll just say that during the lunch hour we've reviewed the transcripts and extra time will not be necessary. I'm confident you'll be glad to hear. I'll now presume -- I'll now resume with where I left off. Your Honours, on the monitors in front of you, you should see a map, this is Exhibit P2110, and this is a map of the areas where the murder operation was carried out. This can be found at the end of volume 2 of the judgement. In the lower right corner you see Srebrenica. I've highlighted it with a box. Above that you can see Bratunac, which I've also highlighted with a box. If you continue up the road beside the river Drina, about halfway up the screen you'll see Zvornik, which is also surrounded by a box. And these are the key areas where Beara was active during the murder operation. Your Honours, Beara has claimed an alibi during this period. This could not be further from the truth. In reality, he was ubiquitous during the formation and implementation of the murder operation, and that's found -- that's noted at paragraphs 1300 and 1318 of the judgement. The following are a very small range of examples of his relevant activities and locations during these times. Firstly, on 11 July, Beara was at the Drina Corps forward command post - this is on the next slide - in Pribicevac, just south of Srebrenica. He was there with fellow JCE member Vujadin Popovic and they reported to Radislav Krstic. If we move to the next slide, you'll see that on 12th July he was seen in the centre of Bratunac with Miroslav Deronjic. On the morning of that same day, 12th July, Popovic and Momir Nikolic had been in the centre of Bratunac, the same town, discussing the murder operation, as set out at paragraph 280 of the judgement. On 13 July, on the next slide, as the prisoners poured into Bratunac and as the larger killings began to occur, Beara's activities intensified. For example, that evening he met Momir Nikolic in the centre of Bratunac and he sent him up to Zvornik to tell Drago Nikolic that the prisoners would be sent there to be killed. That same evening he met at the SDS offices in Bratunac with people, including Miroslav Deronjic, to discuss the murder operation. Beara and Deronjic argued, as found by the Chamber, the issue was not whether to kill the prisoners; the issue was where to kill the prisoners. And that's noted at paragraph 1060. Beara has claimed that the Chamber's findings in this regard are based solely on the evidence of Deronjic. This is incorrect. At the outset, in response to his challenges to the credibility and reliability of Deronjic's evidence, I should note that that has been confirmed at the appellate level, as you'll be aware, the admission of Deronjic's evidence. Furthermore, in disputing this finding by the Trial Chamber, Beara ignores that there are multiple witnesses and other materials corroborating the Chamber's findings. These include Momir Nikolic, PW-161, PW-170, the accused Borovcanin, and others. And these are set out in paragraphs 1264 to 1270 of the judgement. For example, Momir Nikolic testified that, on this evening, he observed Beara and Deronjic at the SDS office in Bratunac. He noted that they were arguing and they were arguing about where to carry out the murder operation. That's in the judgement at paragraphs 1266 to 1270. PW-161 also testified about meetings at these same SDS offices, where the killing of prisoners and the burial was discussed. The subject of the meetings that PW-161 was involved in was the burial of the prisoners murdered at Kravica. And that's set out at paragraphs 438 and 1267 to 1268 of the judgement. And PW-161 confirmed that Beara was present at these meetings. PW-161 knew Beara prior to this occasion so he could recognise him at this time. At today's hearing, Beara has argued and focused on the discrepancies in the "specifics" of the witnesses' accounts of these meetings on the evening of 13 July in Bratunac. However, the Chamber expressly took these into account at footnote 4167. It's unsurprising that the different witnesses have differences as to what they specifically observed. As Deronjic himself stated, people were coming and going at the time during these discussions on the evening of 13 July. And that's in P3139 at transcript page 6448. In making in his arguments, Beara also misunderstands the concept of corroboration. It's well established that testimonies do not need to be exactly identical in order to corroborate each other. The key is that they lend probative weight to the other piece of evidence, and that can be found, for example, in Munyakazi appeal judgement, paragraph 103, and in the Mrksic appeal judgement at paragraph 125. And the assessment of corroboration is a factor falling squarely within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, and that's in the Limaj appeal judgement, paragraph 203. Beara's focus on the specific details of these meetings ignores the common thread running through these witnesses' evidence, which is that there was a series of meetings at the SDS offices that Beara was present at and involved in to discuss the murder operation. Moreover, Beara's activities that evening fit with his following movements the next day. For example, on 14 July, as you see in the next slide, he met with Popovic and Drago Nikolic at the Standard barracks, and as found by the Chamber, they met to discuss the murder operation. That same day, Beara went to Grbavci school in Orahovac which is also near Zvornik. At the time, many hundreds of prisoners had been brought to the school on the night before and on 14 July and were detained in horrific conditions. The prisoners were then murdered a short distance from the school. Again on 14 July, Beara was at Petkovci, another location near Zvornik. He was there overseeing the detention, transport, execution, and burial of over 800 prisoners. That's paragraph 1279 of the judgement. On 15 July, Beara continued to drive forward the murder operation. At 10.00 a.m. he was recorded calling Radislav Krstic, who was the commander of the Drina Corps, and asking for more soldiers to assist with the murder operation. He used a euphemistic code, referring to parcels that had to be distributed. The Chamber found that this conversation concerned troops to assist with the killing operation. This next slide contains an excerpt from the intercepted conversation; this is P1179. The speaker designated with a B is Beara. He explains his exasperation at not receiving the additional troops that he needed. He then made a telling statement which I've highlighted with a box. He says: "I don't know what to do. I mean it, Krle. There are still some 3.500 'parcels' that I have to distribute and I have no solution." Now, Beara disputes the authenticity of this intercept; however, it was authenticated by three separate intercept operators who all identified Beara and Krstic as the participants, as set out at paragraph 1236.
