On the next slide you can see that the same day as this conversation was intercepted and he was recorded talking about distributing over 3.000 prisoners, there were indeed somewhere between 2- and 3.000 prisoners detained at nearby locations, at the Rocevic and Kula and the Pilica cultural centre. As the Chamber noted in paragraphs 504 to 550, these prisoners were indeed executed that day and in the following days. On 16 July, the day after he had called for more troops to assist with the killing operation, he personally went to Kula school where hundreds of prisoners were detained. They were taken to nearby Branjevo Farm and executed. Now, there are a few points that become immediately apparent from this slide show. The first is that Beara's alibi is untrue. This evidence supporting these findings, as I've mentioned, comes from a variety of sources and was validly assessed by the Trial Chamber. The second point, which is quite important, is the slides show how his movements shadow the killings as they begin down in Bratunac and as they move north up to Zvornik. This reflects his central role in organising and implementing the killing operation. Third, it's significant that he's present at these detention locations because the conditions there were appalling. The heat was stifling for the prisoners, the rooms were overcrowded, and frequent beatings occurred. In many instances, prisoners were killed right there at these various detention locations. Beara's callous disregard for the suffering of these Bosnian Muslim prisoners in these conditions and his relentless focus on killing as many of them as possible as quickly as possible are confirmation of his murderous and genocidal intent. I'll now turn to address some of his challenges to the reliability of the evidence against him. Very briefly, it's necessary to note a couple of words about the appellate standards at this stage. When you review his submissions, you'll see that almost all of them were raised at trial. This ignores the relevant jurisprudence, which holds that an appeal is not an opportunity for a trial de novo. Your Honours, in relation to the numerous witnesses that identified Beara during this period, he argues, firstly, that the witnesses' identifications are flawed; and secondly, that many of the witnesses colluded together to falsely implicate him in these events. Turning first to his identification arguments, and these are contained in ground 10 of his brief. The Trial Chamber set out the appropriate standards in the judgement for assessing identification evidence at paragraph 55, and it analysed the identification evidence and his arguments in detail at paragraphs 1219 to 1229. His arguments amount to mere disagreements of the Trial Chamber's assessments. His arguments are erroneous. Many of the witnesses knew Beara and were able to recognise him, these include PW-161, Milorad Bircakovic, Miroslav Deronjic, and Momir Nikolic, for example. Other witnesses were introduced to him by name, such as Egbers who I've mentioned, PW-162, PW-104, and PW-165. Beara was an extremely high-level figure in the VRS. He was the head of the security administration, he had the rank of colonel. He's a distinctive-looking individual. The idea that somebody was walking around masquerading as Colonel Beara at meetings with local officials in various places is simply untenable. Moving to his second argument concerning witness collusion. In ground 5 he names a group of local officials that he claims conspired against him, these include Deronjic, PW-161, PW-162, Ljubisav Simic, and Zlatan Celanovic. These arguments are a direct repeat of his trial arguments, as you'll see, for example, at para 164 of his brief, and the Chamber addressed these in detail. As the Chamber found, there was no basis for his claims and the testimony of these witnesses does not suggest falsification. Fundamentally, he conflates two things. He conflates the fact that some of these witnesses knew each other and talked to each other with the contention that they actually falsely created their evidence to implicate him. Moreover, his arguments are self-contradictory. He includes Zlatan Celanovic as one of the members of this supposed conspiracy against him; however, later in his brief, he argues that Celanovic's evidence is, in fact, exculpatory. You can see that, for instance, at paragraph 111. This is inconsistent. He also argues that there was a separate conspiracy against him amongst VRS witnesses, Ostoja Stanisic and Marko Milosevic, who both gave evidence concerning his presence at the Petkovci school on 14 July. The Chamber addressed these arguments in detail and found that these witnesses were straightforward in their answers. He shows no reason to interfere with the Trial Chamber's reasonable exercise of its discretion. And as a final point and a very important one in relation to his identification arguments and his witness collusion arguments which are at the core of his appeal, it's important to note that the corroborating evidence comes from a variety of sources. For example, there's the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook. As set out at paragraph 1276 of the judgement, it records on 14 July: "Colonel Beara is coming in (the following) order to Orovoc," namely, Orahovac, "Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica." The Defence haven't mentioned that today or yesterday, but this is a telling entry in a separate document. 14 July is right during the midst of the large-scale killings, and these are four of the locations where those killings occurred. Your Honours, there's also the intercepts and I've mentioned one of them already. They were recorded contemporaneously but they continue to speak loud and clear as to his murderous and genocidal intent. The Chamber took these into account and validly assessed their weight. Your Honours, the trial -- Beara fails to show any error in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the reliability of the evidence against him. With those statements in mind, I'll now turn to his arguments concerning the joint criminal enterprise findings and the genocide findings. Looking first to the joint criminal enterprise findings, the Chamber found that Beara was a driving force behind the murder operation to kill the Bosnian Muslim men and boys from Srebrenica. It held that the murder operation implicated personnel and units from the Main Staff of the VRS through to the corps and the brigade level, and that the security branch, of which Beara was the head of the security administration, played a heavy hand throughout. The evidence shows that he made multiple contributions to the joint criminal enterprise. As I've already outlined, he identified locations to implement the murder plan, he secured personnel and equipment for the killings and burials, he oversaw the execution at individual killing sites, and he co-ordinated with other participants in the killing operation, including Popovic and Drago Nikolic. He was omnipresent, in the words of the Chamber, throughout the scenes of the mass killings; that's paragraph 1300. Beara disputes these joint criminal enterprise findings by essentially repeating his trial arguments and seeking to re-interpret the Chamber's findings on the evidence. Rather than addressing all of his arguments, I'll focus on three that arise repeatedly throughout his brief and he's touched on in his oral arguments. First, he argues that the Chamber erred in concluding that he was involved in the murder operation from 12th July. He contends that this was an inference and that the Chamber failed to provide reasons for it. For instance, you can find that at paragraph 178 of his brief. In this respect, his arguments are misconceived. First, it's well-established that a Trial Chamber can reach an inferential finding as long as it is the only reasonable possibility on the basis of the evidence; and second, the Trial Chamber provided its reasons for exactly why this was the case. It explained that on the morning of 12th of July, Popovic, who was subordinate to Beara in the security branch, was discussing the murder operation in Bratunac. And as I mentioned, Beara was in Bratunac that same day. By this stage, the order for the murder operation had emanated from Mladic, the commander of the VRS, as set out in paragraph 1071. The fact that Mladic, who was superior to Beara, and Popovic, who was his immediate subordinate, were both aware of the murder operation, in conjunction with the role played by the security branch of the murder operation from its beginning, is strong evidence that he was aware of the murder operation as well. And as the Chamber explained, it's consistent with his behaviour over the following days. Again, he fails to show that this was an unreasonable finding. Moving to his second argument concerning the joint criminal enterprise findings, this is his claim that the logistical assistance he provided in relation to burials and personnel related to Muslims killed during combat. And you can see this, for instance, in grounds 6, 15, and 19. This combat-related assistance claim is incorrect. In fact, the evidence shows that his assistance related directly to the murder and burial of detained Bosnian Muslims. The execution of detained people cannot be classified as combat activity. For example, I've mentioned that on 13 July Beara met with PW-161 at the SDS offices and sent him -- and PW-161 participated in the burying of the Kravica warehouse victims at Glogova. Subsequently, Popovic ordered the reburial of these same victims buried at Glogova as found at paragraphs 603 and 1158 to 1161. If these were combat-related victims, why was Beara's fellow JCE member ordering their reburial? Further support for the Chamber's findings that his assistance did not relate to combat-related victims comes from Witness PW-104. He testified that on 14 July he was called for a briefing with Beara at the Standard barracks at Zvornik. Beara said to PW-104: "We have a lot of prisoners and it is very hard for us to control them. They're at various locations in the Zvornik municipality. We have to get rid of them. I expect assistance from the municipality."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: PW-104 testified that by getting rid of them, Beara meant burying the bodies of prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. Thank you for the reminder. Again, there is nothing combat-related about executing prisoners. Moving to Beara's third argument concerning the joint criminal enterprise findings, this is his claim that he only intended the exchange of the detained Bosnian Muslims and not their execution. And this is raised, for example, in grounds 6 and 7 of his brief. This is contradicted by numerous sources of evidence, showing his willing participation in the murder operation, as set out in the judgement at paragraphs 1255 to 1288, and I won't go back through those again. These specific pieces of evidence that he relies on to support his exchange argument do not bear the weight that he seeks to place on them. He's talked about document 7D2D642. I believe earlier on the transcript this came out as 7D2D64, but it should be 7D2D642, just for references purposes. Now, this is the summary of an intercept at 11.25 a.m. on 13 July 1995. It refers to Beara being involved with the transport of some Muslim prisoners from Kasaba to the Batkovic detention camp. Now, the Chamber addressed this in detail and found it does not vitiate the evidence showing his involvement in the murder operation. This is a two-sentence summary. It doesn't contain the actual conversation and we don't have the actual conversation in any other form. We don't know who the other participant in the conversation was and we don't know the specific terms that were used. What we do know is that the murder operation was supposed to be carried out in secret, as set out in 1057 to 1058 of the judgement. And we know that Beara was aware of the vulnerability of phones to interception. We also know that rather than exchanging prisoners, Beara sent thousands of them to their deaths, as set out at paragraph 1283, for example. The next piece of evidence that he repeatedly cites in support of his exchange argument is the testimony of Zlatan Celanovic. Celanovic recounted Beara saying on 13 July that if the Bosnian Muslims detained at Bratunac made it through the night, they would be sent to Kladanj the next day. Beara claims this shows he thought they would be exchanged. However, he ignores the relevant circumstances. First, Beara was at the SDS offices that same evening, 13 July, advocating the murder of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners, not their exchange. Second, as I've mentioned, the VRS was required to carry out the murder operation in secrecy. The Chamber noted these considerations in the judgement. In these circumstances, it's unsurprising that he refrained from openly discussing the murder operation with Zlatan Celanovic, who was a lawyer with no rank attached to the Bratunac Brigade. Additionally, Momir Nikolic said that this supposed sending of some Muslim men to Kladanj was "a propaganda exercise." That's in his statement C00001, page 3. Momir Nikolic explained that some Muslim men were even put onto buses with the women and children on Potocari and sent towards Kladanj for the benefit of the Dutch troops and for Serb TV, but then removed from the buses before they reached Kladanj. And this information was acknowledged in the judgement at paragraphs 334, 336, and 338. In light of the circumstances, his exchange argument is unconvincing. What these two pieces of evidence do confirm is, again, that his alibi was untrue. They show he was in the area and that his activities did relate to the Bosnian Muslim prisoners. Your Honours, I've only touched on a small fraction of the evidence showing his involvement and contributions to the joint criminal enterprise, and it's set out in detail in the judgement. The Chamber reached entirely reasonable findings in convicting him for his participation in these crimes. Having addressed these arguments, I'll now turn to his challenges to the genocide convictions. In ground 19 he argues that he did not have genocidal intent, and you've heard again a development on these arguments this morning. However, Beara fails to show any error, legal or factual, with the trial judgement, and I should note that in his brief his arguments are substantially primarily factual arguments on this ground. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 856 that: "The scale and nature of the murder operation, the targeting of the victims, the systematic and organized manner in which it was carried out, and the plain intention to eliminate every Bosnian Muslim male who was captured or surrendered proves beyond reasonable doubt that members of the Bosnian Serb forces, including members of the VRS Main Staff and Security Branch, intended to destroy the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia as a group." Beara was involved in the murder operation in all its key aspects and he had a clear overall picture of its massive scale and scope. As the Chamber succinctly summarised - this is paragraph 1314: "His vigorous efforts to organise locations and sites, recruit personnel, secure equipment and oversee executions all evidence his grim determination to kill as many as possible as quickly as possible." Addressing the arguments you've heard this morning, the Chamber found that the killing operation of many thousand Bosnian Muslim men and boys targeted exclusively on the basis of their ethnicity, was sufficient in and of itself to infer genocidal intent on the part of certain perpetrators. That's important. It was enough in and of itself. It then also referred to the forcible transfer operation being consistent with that finding but not necessary, consistent. On the totality of the evidence, it concluded that Beara was one of the individuals who possessed genocidal intent. The Defence have claimed that this is inconsistent with the findings in the Krstic appeal judgement, and that is incorrect. The Defence ignored that the Krstic appeal judgement confirmed that the killing of many thousand men and boys from the Srebrenica enclave was sufficient to infer genocidal intent. And I'll read some of the paragraphs where it sets this out. We can start with paragraph 21 of the Krstic appeal judgement. "The Trial Chamber determined that Radislav Krstic had the intent to kill the Srebrenica Bosnian Muslim men of military age. This finding is one of intent to commit the requisite genocidal act - in this case, the killing of the members of the protected group, prohibited by Article 4(2)(a) of the Statute. From this intent to kill, the Trial Chamber also drew the further inference that Krstic shared the genocidal intent of some members of the VRS Main Staff to destroy a substantial part of the targeted group, the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica." They continue at para 26: "The main evidence underlying the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the VRS forces intended to eliminate all the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica was the massacre by the VRS of all men of military age from that community." Paragraph 27: "The killing of the military-aged men was, assuredly, a physical destruction, and given the scope of the killings the Trial Chamber could legitimately draw the inference that their extermination was motivated by a genocidal intent." Your Honours, the Defence has said that the victims were a very small percentage of the overall Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia and even of the overall Bosnian Muslim population. The Krstic Appeals Chamber addressed this consideration, and they noted that the Trial Chamber was entitled to consider the long-term impact of the elimination of 7- to 8.000 men from Srebrenica on the survival of that community. This is paragraph 28 of the Krstic appeal judgement. They noted that: "... given the patriarchal character of the Bosnian Muslim society in Srebrenica, the destruction of such a sizeable number of men would 'inevitably result in the physical disappearance of the Bosnian Muslim population at Srebrenica.'" They continued: "The physical destruction of the men therefore had severe procreative implications for the Srebrenica Muslim community, potentially consigning the community to extinction ..." It's simply not a fair reading of the Krstic appeal judgement to say that the Appeals Chamber required participation in forcible transfer to infer genocidal intent. It doesn't say that. Your Honours, Judge Shahabuddeen's dissent has been cited. That doesn't reflect the majority's reasoning. That's why it's called a dissent. It cannot be taken for that proposition. In any event, the Chamber found that Beara was, in fact, aware of the forcible transfer operation, he knew that these killings did not occur in a vacuum, and you can see that in paragraph 1307. You can also see it in the Chamber's findings concerning the chapeau elements for crimes against humanity. Beara knew these killings were part of a widespread and systematic attack. Importantly, the Defence arguments also ignore a significant part of Beara's conviction, the basis for his conviction. And this is the serious bodily and mental harm he caused to the survivors of these massacres. The Chamber found that the underlying acts of genocide included killing and serious bodily and mental harm, not only to the victims of the killings, but also to the male survivors and also to the surviving family members and loved ones of the killed. That's the women, the children, the other people separated from the victims. These are set out at paragraphs 842 to 847. The Chamber found that Beara "committed the underlying act of killing members of the group, and through this killing, inflicted serious bodily and mental harm on the families of the victims and the survivors of the executions ..." That's paragraph 1310. So his actions had implications far broader than the immediate murder victims. Your Honours, you should reject the Defence arguments based on the Krstic appeal judgement. They're inconsistent with their written arguments and they simply do not reflect the state of the jurisprudence at this Tribunal. An additional argument that Beara makes in his brief is that: "Any actions taken by Beara with regard to the military-aged men in the enclave were lawful, combat-related activities against a perceived military threat." This claim turns the law on its head. The suggestion there was anything lawful about systematically murdering thousands of men and boys who were detained and murdering them on an ethnic basis cannot be countenanced. Moreover, the Trial Chamber was well aware of this argument. It found at paragraphs 860 to 861 of the judgement that the murder operation went well beyond any response to a legitimate threat. It noted that no serious effort was made to distinguish between civilians and soldiers. It found that any screening efforts were so sporadic and void of superior direction or supervision that one cannot derive a sincere intention on the part of the Bosnian Serb forces to carry out a legitimate screening operation. That's footnote 3453. Moreover, it noted that the Bosnian Serb forces killed young boys, old men with walking sticks, some women, and even a mentally handicapped man. Many of the victims had their hands tied behind their backs when they were killed and were blindfolded. What kind of military threat did they present? Many of the victims had nothing to do with the military. But what all the victims did have is one thing in common: They were Bosnian Muslims. And that's who was really being targeted here. The Chamber's finding that the purpose went beyond any military motivation is indeed consistent with the findings upheld by the Appeals Chamber in Krstic as set out at paragraphs 26 to 27 of the appeal judgement. Beara's challenge to these findings is simply an attempt at revisionism to try and avoid facing full justice for his actions. He intended to kill the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia and that's the finding entered in the judgement on the basis of the evidence. Your Honours, in his reply he refers to the judgement of Niyitigeka from the ICTR. Now, if you look at Niyitigeka, it doesn't say that military motivations preclude a finding of genocidal intent. In fact, it stands for the opposite proposition. The Appeals Chamber held at paragraphs 49 to 53 that additional motivations, such as personal or military motives, do not preclude a finding of genocide. At the ICTY the jurisprudence has taken a similar line. In the Jelisic appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber held that the existence of a personal motive, such as economic gain, political advantage, or some other form of power, does not preclude a finding of genocidal intent. That's at paragraph 49. The evidence shows that, in reality, Beara engaged in the mass killing of defenceless Bosnian Muslims with ruthless calculation. He organised the systematic killing of every Bosnian Muslim his forces could get their hands on. His own words provide further evidence of his genocidal intent. For example, in P1130, you'll see that on 13 July, when he was informed that Bosnian Muslims were killing themselves, he said: "You mean they are doing it amongst themselves? Well, excellent. Just let them continue. Fuck it." There are other examples I've referred to, examples where he said he was getting rid of prisoners and he needed the assistance of the municipality, and where he said he had 3.500 parcels to distribute, which the Chamber found meant Bosnian Muslim prisoners to execute. As the Trial Chamber observed at paragraph 1316, these words capture clearly and succinctly the state of mind of a man bent on destroying a group by killing all the members of it within his reach. On the basis of the totality of the evidence, the Chamber's findings are entirely reasonable. The second ground I'll address in relation to the genocide conviction is Beara's argument that the Trial Chamber erred by finding that the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia constituted a substantial part of the Bosnian Muslims as a whole. And he challenges this in ground 21 of his brief. He argues that the Trial Chamber ignored the size of this part of the group, and under the law, as you're well aware, the targeted part of the group must constitute a substantial part of the whole group. When Beara says that the Chamber ignored the size of the group, that's not correct. The Chamber looked first to the size of the targeted group and it noted that it was a relatively small percentage of the overall Bosnian Muslim population. At this stage, mid-1995, there were over 40.000 Bosnian Muslims crowded, herded, into the enclave, which is actually not an insignificant number of people in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. Nonetheless, as the Appeals Chamber has held in Krstic, the importance of the Muslim community of Srebrenica is not captured solely by its size. Other relevant considerations can be taken into account, and the Trial Chamber indeed did so at paragraph 865. It looked at the concentration of the Muslim inhabitants of the region into the enclave. The elimination of this population would eradicate the entire region of its Muslim population. It looked at the strategic importance of the enclave. The capture and ethnic purification of Srebrenica would seriously jeopardise the efforts of the Bosnian Muslim state to ensure its viability. And it looked at the emblematic significance of eliminating the Srebrenica Bosnian Muslims in the face of the international assurances of safety. This would serve as a potent example to all Bosnian Muslims of their vulnerability and defencelessness in the face of the Bosnian Serb military forces. During these events, thousands were murdered, tens of thousands were expelled, and the Bosnian Muslim collective consciousness was indelibly harmed. Those who survived suffered profound physical and psychological harm as a result of the murder operation. The Chamber appropriately found that this mass killing, the largest in Europe since World War II, constituted genocide. The Chamber's approach adheres to the Appeals Chamber's findings in Krstic and adheres to the findings of the International Court of Justice in the Bosnia genocide case at paragraphs 290 to 297. Beara was one of those most responsible for the genocide perpetrated against the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. The Chamber properly convicted him, after giving a full hearing to his arguments, on the basis of the evidence. His conviction and the sentence of life imprisonment provide at least a small measure of justice for the victims, both living and deceased, in the face of the massive crimes for which he is responsible. Your Honours, the Defence have said a few words about sentencing. Our arguments are set out in our brief in this respect. Suffice to say, the Trial Chamber noted that these mitigating circumstances were of limited weight, and in the face of his high level of culpability for such grave crimes, a sentence of life imprisonment was entirely appropriate. Anything less would be manifestly inadequate, in our submission. In summary, Beara has challenged every finding against him. At the core of his arguments is the claim there was a vast conspiracy to falsely implicate him in these events. This claim is thoroughly discredited by the evidence. It's discredited by a variety of witnesses, by documents, and by his own words in intercepted conversations. This powerful evidence points in one direction and that's Beara's responsibility for the mass killings and genocide of the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. Your Honours should dismiss his arguments and uphold his convictions and sentence. If you have no further questions, that concludes my submissions, and I would pass over to Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I shall deal with Your Honours' question posed to the parties, and my apologies to the interpreters for my speed yesterday. I will make every effort to be slow today. I hope it doesn't become too slow. The question that Your Honours asked is discussed whether the trial record supports a finding that the necessary link existed between the principal perpetrators of the killings in Jadar River and in Trnovo and Beara; and then secondly, more generally, whether this link existed between the principal perpetrators of crimes who were not necessarily members of the VRS and members of the JCE to murder. And we note in particular the footnote to item 10, where Your Honours list specific aspects of the trial judgement at paragraphs 794.1, .2, .7, and .9, and we will address those. Your Honours, of course, in terms of the law, it's well established that crimes committed by persons who are not necessarily JCE members themselves can be attributed to JCE members if the necessary link between the perpetrators and one or more of the JCE members is demonstrated. That's obviously referring to Brdjanin at 413, and Martic at 168, Krajisnik at 225, all appeals judgements. And non-JCE members in these scenarios frequently referred to as tools. Past cases at the Tribunal here have recognised a non-exhaustive list of ways in which the link can be made between the principal perpetrators and the JCE members. And those are referred to again in Brdjanin at 365 and 411; Martic at 168; and Stakic at 65, again all appeals judgements. But in broad terms, one of the ways is where a member of the JCE is in a hierarchical relationship with the principal perpetrators or where the principal perpetrators are working in close co-operation with forces that are under the authority of a JCE member. And Your Honours will recall from the Martic appeals judgement and Krajisnik appeals judgement, Your Honours looked carefully at how those links were established because the Appeals Chamber considered the Trial Chamber in parts in those cases had some difficulty articulating that link. We understand that is where Your Honours are driving with the question today. Of course, it's important to remember that the question of whether a link exists in the particular circumstances of the case is a factual question, and consequently, deference will apply to that factual determination where it has been made unless it's so unreasonable that no Trial Chamber could reach that conclusion. Again, the relevant jurisprudence set out in Brdjanin, Martic, and Krajisnik. I'm not going to repeat it again. Popovic Trial Chamber understood that because it referred to this governing law at paragraphs 1029 to 1030 in its judgement. So it was well aware of what was required. In relation to the Jadar River, turning first to that, the Chamber found that on the 13th of July, 1995, 15 Bosnian Muslims were killed at the Jadar River. Perpetrators were found to be Bosnian Serb forces which it defines in the judgement, in fact, and it included at least one member of the MUP, Nenad Deronjic. That's found at judgement paragraph 408. Paragraph 199 of the appeal brief, Beara accepts that the perpetrators of the killing incident included members of the police in his brief at paragraph 199. Your Honours, in relation to the Jadar River killing and the other killings in and around Bratunac, the Trial Chamber held that: "Common elements, including the units involved," Bratunac Brigade, "the method and means by which the killings were carried out, and the time-frame within which they occurred bring these events within the scope of the common purpose." That's at judgement 1074. So, in other words, they understood the totality of what was happening on the ground at the time in making their determination. And the trial record provides ample support for the finding and demonstrates, for example, that the Bratunac Brigade was closely co-operating with the MUP units involved in the killings. Of course, the Bratunac Brigade and the other VRS forces sitting underneath the command of Ratko Mladic, one of the named JCE members. PW-112, the one survivor of the Jadar River killings and a key witness for the incident, was together with other members of the column on the 13th of July, when he was arrested by MUP members along the Bratunac to Konjevic Polje road. That's referred to in the judgement at paragraph 390. The Trial Chamber found that there was a single operation by Bosnian Serb forces on the 13th of July along that road, the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, resulting in the surrender or capture of many hundreds of Bosnian Muslims from the column. Bosnian Serb forces involved in the operation included the Bratunac Brigade and various MUP units, referred to in the judgement at 1458, 365, and 376 to 389. MUP members involved in the operation were under either the authority of the VRS or closely co-operating with them. For example, Your Honours can find reference in the testimony of Mirko Trivic at trial transcript 11844, who was the commander of the Romanija Brigade, testifying that the Bratunac and Milici Brigades, in co-operation with MUP forces, were ordered to secure the Bratunac to Konjevic Polje road and the Konjevic Polje to Milici road. It's in the judgement at paragraph 376. Similarly, P00148, a Drina Corps intelligence service report of the 12th of July, signed by Tolimir, notes that the commands of the Bratunac, Zvornik, and Milici Brigades were to act in co-operation with the police in securing the roads, including the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Consistent with this, Momir Nikolic confirmed that on the 12th of July and the early morning of the 13th, through intelligence reports and other information, he was made aware that VRS and MUP forces were capturing Muslim men in the area of Konjevic Polje. That's in his statement of facts exhibited at C1. Bosnian Muslims captured during this operation were killed in and around Bratunac or transported out of the -- to the Zvornik area and killed in locations there, referred to in the judgement at 1449 to 53. Your Honours, the way in which PW-112 and other victims of the Jadar River incident were apprehended, interrogated, and then significantly taken by bus to be killed by the Bosnian Serb forces, including MUP units, fits with the operation and the other killing incidents that were carried out that day, such as the Kravica warehouse murders, also involving VRS and MUP forces, killing men from the detained column. I refer Your Honours to the judgement at 408 and also 390. Your Honours, PW-112 was captured by MUP members, he was interrogated at a facility used by the VRS 5th Engineer Battalion, as shown in Exhibit P00686, and was taken together with other victims later to the execution site at the Jadar River on a bus. The perpetrators, at least one of whom was identified as a MUP member, wearing military camouflage uniforms. Your Honours, in our submission, it was clear that the Trial Chamber accepted that this incident was part of the operations by Bosnian Serb forces, and in the totality of the circumstances, it was appropriate to link it to one of the JCE members, in this case Ratko Mladic as commander of the VRS forces, either directly or through the mode of close co-operation, indicating that attribution thereby to a JCE member is made and thereby liability established across to Beara for his part as a JCE member. Of course, such close co-operation between units and VRS forces is sufficient, as I've already said, in -- established in Martic. Your Honours, then moving on to the Trnovo incident, Your Honour, this is a slightly different set of circumstances. The Chamber found that in July 1995, some six Bosnian men and boys were killed near Trnovo town, approximately 150 kilometres from Zvornik, by a Serbian MUP unit called the Skorpions. That's in the judgement at 597 to 599 and also referred at 794.18. The victims were all Bosnian Muslim men from Srebrenica, judgement 1080, and they were last seen by their families in the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995. That's in Exhibit P03248 and there's a stipulation. At least one of the victims was at one point part of the column. That's referred to in footnote 2166. The Chamber held that the killings at Trnovo fell within the scope of the JCE to murder, stating that it would be "an unreasonable inference that within the same relative time-period in an adjoining area there was a separate, distinct murder operation targeting precisely the same victims." That's at trial judgement paragraph 1080. Your Honours, in light of the circumstances of the victims, the Chamber's finding was reasonable. The Trial Chamber correctly observed that the victims were from the same group as the other victims of the JCE 1 murder incidents in and around Bratunac and Zvornik. Moreover, there is some evidence on the record showing that the Bosnian -- that the Skorpions were part of Bosnian Serb MUP forces working together with the VRS in Trnovo in July 1995, and we refer you to Exhibit P03794 and also to transcript reference 26860, together with other references relating to the brigade structures at trial judgement 185 and 244. Your Honour, the combination of victims coming from Srebrenica and the Skorpions operating with MUP forces in concert with the VRS is powerful support for the incident falling within the JCE's common purpose, and such co-operation between the Skorpions and the MUP units together with VRS forces in the context is sufficient for JCE attribution, as set out previously. I turn to the next part of the question. I'm sorry it takes a little while to get through these incidents. Opportunistic killings are the second part of Your Honours' question referring to 794.1 and.7 at the Vuk Karadzic school. Your Honours, in paragraph 794.1, the Chamber found that on the 12th and the 13th of July, between 40 and 80 Bosnian Muslim prisoners were taken from a hangar behind the Vuk Karadzic school and killed. This is in the judgement at 452 to 55. And in paragraph 794.7, the Chamber found that between the 13th and the 15th of July, an unknown number of Bosnian Muslim men were killed inside and outside the same school, again in the judgement 460 to 63, and of course the paragraph referred. Your Honours, VRS members were directly involved in both the guarding and the execution of the prisoners. There's reference in the trial judgement 406. At 406, the Bosnian Muslim prisoners in Bratunac town on the 12th to the 13th of July were guarded by members of the Bosnian Serb forces, including military policemen of the Bratunac Brigade. They were working together with members of the MUP in those activities, and evidence underlying this finding includes that of military police Mile Janjic, referred to at footnote 1424 of the judgement; and Momir Nikolic explained in Exhibit C1 at page 6 that it was decided at a meeting on the evening of 13 July at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters that the prisoners in Bratunac should continue to be guarded by elements of the Bratunac Brigade military police, various civilian MUP forces, and armed volunteers from the Bratunac town. That's at judgement paragraph 406. Your Honours, it's inconceivable that those activities were not being carried out together and as part of the whole operation. The perpetrators of the killings of the prisoners from the hangar behind the school were Bosnian Serb forces, including soldiers in camouflage uniform, as set out in the evidence at PW-169, an example at transcript 17324 to 17326. Indeed, Mladic himself came to the hangar on the morning of the 13th of July and gave instructions to ten members of Bosnian Serb forces who were guarding prisoners there, as set out in paragraph 402 of the judgement. Your Honours, the perpetrators of the killings of prisoners held inside the Vuk Karadzic school and outside on buses were a mix of soldiers and policemen, as testified to by Ahmo Hasic, one of the survivors, at transcript 1180 to 1181, and 1188. And we refer Your Honours also to trial judgement 461. Beara himself walked past the buses parked outside the Vuk Karadzic school on the 13th of July and saw prisoners detained in and around the school, referenced in the judgement at paragraph 1262. Your Honours, based on the evidence, the killings in and around the Vuk Karadzic school are linked to the JCE in several ways. The killings were part of a joint operation by the VRS and MUP forces in Bratunac. VRS members specifically being involved in them. And JCE members such as Mladic and Beara on hand guiding and monitoring the work of Bosnian Serb forces. Consequently, these killings are not separate and distinct from the VRS/MUP operation to detain the Muslim prisoners. And the findings that the killings were foreseeable consequences of the implementation of the JCE to murder are thus entirely reasonable. At 794.2, moving on to the next incident, this is another opportunistic killing, this time in Potocari. On the 13th July 1995, nine Bosnian Muslim men were killed in a field near a stream about 500 metres distant from the DutchBat compound in Potocari, judgement 354 to 59. And one Bosnian Muslim --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You are kindly asked to slow down for the purposes of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I failed. I'm very sorry. I was doing my best. Your Honours, just dealing with one Bosnian Muslim man was taken behind a building near the White House at Potocari at killed, judgement 354 to 359. The Chamber reasonably found that it was the Bosnian Serb forces who killed the nine men found near the DutchBat compound. Potocari was taken over on the 12th July by VRS and MUP units operating together, as found at trial judgement paragraph 302. The MUP units who participated in the take-over of Potocari included the Jahorina recruits and the 1st PJP Company from Zvornik, both units under the command of Borovcanin. That's found in the judgement at paragraph 185. Indeed, Borovcanin was present in Potocari on the 12th July as was Mladic, moving constantly through the area, referred to again in the judgement, and seen personally handing out food. By the morning of the 13th of July, Bosnian Serb forces fully controlled Potocari and not even DutchBat could walk freely, as set out in the judgement at paragraph 302 to 305 and 357. In those circumstances, it was entirely reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that the killings in Potocari were committed by Bosnian Serb forces and were foreseeable consequences of the JCE to murder. Indeed, when looking at the killings of the nine men, DutchBat officers found that they were still warm when they examined them. They were fired on by Bosnian Serb forces, that's DutchBat themselves were fired upon, as noted in the judgement at 355 and 356. And again, the perpetrators who killed the Muslim men behind the White House were observed by DutchBat forces to be Serb soldiers wearing typical camouflage uniforms, matching those of other Bosnian Serb forces who controlled Potocari at the time. Suggesting they observed the killing itself, they saw the men being taken behind by uniformed soldiers. Given the involvement of forces under the authority of JCE members such as Mladic in joint operation with the MUP and given his -- Mladic's personal involvement in directing Bosnian Serb forces in relation to those detentions in Potocari, the Chamber properly found that the killings were linked to the implementation of the JCE. Your Honours, I've just got one more to deal with. I'm conscious we're coming up to a break. It will take me just a couple of minutes, and then probably it's a good time, if it's suitable to Your Honours, to break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Final incident, 794.9, the Petkovci school. Your Honours, there the Chamber held that on the 14th of July, 1995, several Bosnian Muslim men detained at the Petkovci school were killed. This is in the judgement at 498. This was also charged as an opportunistic killing because the main killing of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners detained at the Petkovci school was carried out at the Petkovci dam. Although there was no specific finding as to the precise identity of the perpetrators for the killings at the Petkovci school, the Chamber found that the killings at the dam and other places were: "... well organised and followed the same pattern: men were detained, transported to an appropriate site, and summarily executed. The Zvornik Brigade Military Police guarded the prisoners prior to their execution, various Zvornik Brigade Battalions were involved, and the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Company buried the bodies." That's in the judgement at 1075. Your Honours, there's abundant evidence showing that the detention and killing of Bosnian Muslims at the Petkovci school was connected with the implementation of the murder operation. Your Honours, in those circumstances it's our submission that the Chamber was perfectly proper to associate this incident with the JCE and attribute it in that way to members of the JCE, including Mladic and Beara. Your Honours, that completes my submission in relation to the question and the Prosecution's submissions in response to Mr. Beara before I completely lose my voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say that's the end of the Prosecution's response?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll take the break and resume at 3.23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear the response for - how many minutes? - 30 minutes, 30 minutes. And when that is over, in accordance with the plan announced yesterday, we move on to the next counsel, so, Mr. Bourgon, don't be caught off guard. Okay. But I see you're ready. You're a good scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you. My initial observation, if I may respectfully submit, that I'm not surprised that the OTP has ignored the crux of our argument submitted orally and in written form. I would have expected at least, instead of a regurgitation of the Trial Chamber's conclusions and factual findings, that they would have addressed why any weight should have been given to the Deronjic evidence. The Trial Chamber's decisions with respect to that evidence is consistent throughout all the findings against Beara. They've criticised me for not understanding the aggravating circumstances, but if you look specifically at the sentence at paragraph 2166, the Trial Chamber utilised that same evidence from Deronjic to find that Beara was cold and calculating. They used the same underlying crimes to now find that he was -- it's an aggravating circumstance. I'm disappointed that they didn't even mention the Deronjic evidence, more so than simply to say that the Appellate Chamber had allowed that evidence to be introduced. We know that the first step is to determine whether it's reliable, the next it provides extraordinary caution to the Trial Chamber to give any weight to it. I believe in our submissions, both orally and in writing, we've at least tried and hopefully established that the Deronjic testimony is infected with numerous defects, inconsistencies, and statements that were only self-serving to Deronjic himself to implicate others. My learned friend talked about our main claim being that there was a collusion. He said there's no evidence of that, none whatsoever. We suggest that the joint criminal enterprise members, if you will, at that time included Deronjic, Momir Nikolic, Mr. Borovcanin, and Dragomir Vasic. We saw in the exhibit that was tendered to the Court or shown to the Court, I should say, 2D -- I mean 7 -- sorry, P886, where MUP expressly states that they're taking the sole responsibility. I tried in the brief minutes that we had to scan through the oral submissions to see if they've even addressed it. They don't. They can't. They refuse to. Whenever - and I totally mean this - whenever there is evidence that falls squarely against a Defence argument, the Prosecution either ridicules it or sweeps it under the rug and gives no adequate consideration. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber below also erred in failing to give a reasoned opinion as to why that evidence should have been given its due weight as other evidence. Collusion. Deronjic, Momir Nikolic, Borovcanin, and Vasic. Do we know what Deronjic was convicted of? Yes, it's in the trial record. We know he was convicted for crimes that he and other members of the Bratunac area, political and MUP, were involved in killings in Bratunac merely two to three years prior to the Srebrenica massacre. We know specifically from his sentencing and his plea agreement that he was convicted for the murders in Glogova. The Prosecution will have you believe that Mr. Beara came to Bratunac and he's the one who searched out and was looking for places to bury prisoners. All he had to do, if that's true, is ask Deronjic: Where did you bury them a couple of years ago? The truth of the matter is that there was collusion because they all worked together, they conspired together, and together they committed crimes merely two to three years ago in that same area. They claim there's nothing to link Deronjic with Momir Nikolic. Sure there is. They don't tell the Trial Chamber that Deronjic and Nikolic are related by marriage. Is that not a relevant fact? It's found at the footnote of the Trial Chamber's decision at 4134. Collusion, indeed. Also in a footnote of the Trial Chamber's decision, it talks about how Deronjic and Nikolic confronted each other and that there was a denial or an argument with respect to whether or not Momir Nikolic was even present at the SDS meetings, the same Momir Nikolic who testified not only inconsistently but changed his testimony, admitted to crimes so that he could get a lesser sentence and then retracted them when they found that there was little or no evidence. So the Prosecution in good faith couldn't even accepted his lies that he committed crimes. He was ready to take responsibility for other crimes just so that he could get a lower sentence. Yes, I believe there was collusion. I believe the evidence suggests that there indeed was collusion; however, that's not the thrust of our argument. Our argument remains that if you strip down the trial judgement's decision and its reasoning by giving no weight or, respectfully, very, very limited weight to the Deronjic testimony and evidence, you'll find that the Trial Chamber had insufficient evidence to establish that Ljubisa Beara was a member of the joint criminal enterprise to murder and that Ljubisa Beara did not significantly contribute to that JCE to murder. Likewise, if we strip down -- and I would have expected them to say: We concede; or in the alternative, if you take away Deronjic's testimony, there's enough there, but they know without Deronjic's testimony there is not just scant evidence. There is some evidence, we believe it's not credible, that's our opinion. There's some evidence that he was present. They mock us indirectly and say: Well, in one part they accept Celanovic, but we do in part alternatively state that if it's true and if this Chamber finds that Celanovic is a credible witness, what did Beara say to him? Nothing criminal? Nothing illegal? Nothing offensive? Nothing that would constitute him or this Trial Chamber to conclude that he was a member who substantially contributed to the JCE. We cannot make alternative arguments, but the Prosecution can. That double standard should not exist and I believe that it does not exist --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise. My learned friend said in his oral statements that Beara was advocating murder. Based on what? The Deronjic evidence. He doesn't tell you that's what he bases it on. I would have hoped that they would have argued that either it should give -- the Trial Chamber should have given it all due weight, as it did, or that it shouldn't have given him any weight or limited weight. They simply ignore it. They state that some certain dissenting opinions don't carry much weight. I cited one from the Tolimir case. But it's not a dissenting opinion, it's a dissenting and separate concurring opinion on what justice and the honourable justice -- Judge Nyambe said. She addressed collusion among witnesses. She addressed witnesses who point the finger at others because they want a reduction in their sentence. She cited to Matthew Hale and she states as follows: "This course of admitting of approver's hath been long disused, and the truth is, that more mischief hath come to good men by these kinds of approvements by false accusations of desperate villains, than benefit to the public by the discovery and convicting of real offenders." She cites to Matthew Hale: "History of the Pleas of the Crown."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What year was the cite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- or the opinion? Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Matthew Hale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically, yes, it's 1800. She goes on to say that centuries' old -- for centuries, Trial Chambers have taken with extreme caution and scrutiny the testimony of people who have been convicted, people who have shown to have an inconsistency, and people who have shown to lie only to cover their own actions. There is, I believe, no greater evidence than the evidence from Dragomir Vasic who plainly on that date states MUP was solely responsible and they took over with the goal of liquidating or killing 8.000 Bosnian men and boys. Just briefly, I want to state that they quoted from an -- two appellate records that said: If someone has a personal motive or even a military motive, it does not preclude genocidal intent. However, however, it indeed raises in the right case, in certain circumstances, in the proper context, it raises reasonable doubt as to genocidal intent. We're not suggesting it precludes it, but it certainly provides an opportunity in the proper context to raise sufficient reasonable doubt. The Prosecution has time and time again said we have failed, that we haven't established things fully and completely. It's not our burden at the trial level. That's why we're suggesting that the Trial Court erred, both factually and legally, and failed in its reasoning when it included the evidence of Borovcanin, of Momir Nikolic, and of Miroslav Deronjic. And we ask that this Court, if you consider the Trial Chamber by looking at their legal and factual findings, you'll find that without the Deronjic testimony that should be thrown out, that there is very little, if any, evidence to implicate Mr. Beara. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be quite brief. The Prosecution's burden in this case was to prove that Mr. Beara had the genocidal intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim community in Srebrenica, which was the relevant part of the group. Mr. Beara's acquittal on the forcible transfer charge negated that general intent, we submit. This is clearly shown by paragraphs 31 and 33 of the Krstic Appeals Chamber opinion which I cited at length this morning and won't repeat here. What I would like to repeat here, though, with Your Honours' permission, very briefly, is that part of Judge Shahabuddeen's partially dissenting opinion -- I want to make one thing clear. The Prosecution said in effect - I don't want to be unfair to them - but in effect they said in effect: Don't pay any attention to that opinion, it's a dissenting opinion. That is a gross oversimplification and it's simply not true. Because the only thing that Judge Shahabuddeen dissented on was his opinion was and he found that General Krstic should have been convicted of genocide. The majority reversed the finding of genocide by the Trial Chamber and found him guilty of aiding and assisting genocide. But on all the relevant considerations of genocidal intent, including the acquittal on the forcible transfer, Judge Shahabuddeen was on all fours with the majority opinion, and I don't think the Prosecution wants us to cite it again and I'll do it very briefly because it's so powerful and it's so convincing and it's so logical and that is this, when he said in paragraph 35: "Thus, standing alone, forcible transfer is not genocide, but in this case the transfer did not stand alone and that indeed is the basis on which the Appeals Chamber rejected the Defence argument that it showed that there was no genocide. It was part - an integral part - of one single scheme to commit genocide, involving killings, forcible transfer, and destruction of homes. In particular, it showed that the intent with which the killings were done was indeed to destroy the Srebrenica part of the Bosnian Muslim group." Colonel Beara was -- Mr. Beara was acquitted on the forcible transfer charge under the rationale of both majority in the Appeals Chamber and Judge Shahabuddeen's opinion, I think it's quite clear that the genocide conviction in this case must fall. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also cited I think portions of the Krstic judgement in which the Chamber said that the genocidal intent could be inferred from the killings themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Excuse me. It went on again in paragraphs 31 and 33 of the opinion, Your Honour, to clarify and amplify that, saying that you had to consider also the forcible transfers because the destruction of the relevant group was the entire Bosnian Muslim community of Eastern Bosnia. That's the 40.000 people. A subpart of that 40.000 was the 5300, whatever figure you want to accept, of the military-aged men. But it was certainly not enough to just consider the military-aged men in that equation. It had to be in connection with the destruction -- but that was the only relevant group or relevant part of the group that was accepted by the Trial Chamber, properly so, and charged by the Prosecution as the relevant part of the group. It embraced the entire community, some of which were killed, military-aged men, and many of which, 25.000 or so, were deported. That was the destruction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves that the Court was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, is that -- just to try to understand exactly which is your submission, it's your point that the targeted group, the part of the group, must include the men targeted for killing and the men targeted for transfer at the same time? And you don't have a group targeting only the men that are targeted to be killed? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, our position, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That when the rule says, the norm says, targeting in -- destruction in whole or in part, that part must comprise both the men in the military age have to be killed and the other part of the population, women and children and elderly people, or that part may include only the men that were targeted to be killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes -- no, Your Honour, it's your first supposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's your first supposition, that the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia comprised the men and the transferred -- forcibly transferred population, the women, children, elderly. And that was the charge of the -- this was nothing that was created by Mr. Beara. That was the charge of the government in this case, that was their indictment, that was the theory of their indictment, and we quoted that one paragraph in the Trial Court's opinion, in which it summarised what the Prosecution's theory was. And that was, indeed, the Prosecution's theory and that was accepted - and we think rightly so - by the Trial Chamber as being the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, comprising the group that I just mentioned. That was the theory of the Prosecution in this case. And by the acquittal again on the forcible transfer charge, that negated genocidal intent because the intent was not to destroy and annihilate the entire Bosnian Muslim group. The intent, if anything, was -- assuming, conceding for a moment arguendo, the intent was to kill the men and that's it. When I say "that's it," I don't say that summarily, I say that with proper seriousness of purpose. But that's the most the intent would show in this case, the most. Murder, extermination, I don't -- my colleague Mr. Ostojic has talked to those issues. But I'm assuming arguendo that if there's going to be any conviction in this case, assuming arguendo that you reject, let's say, Mr. Ostojic's argument, it would be for murder and for extermination but not genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you perhaps elaborate on how you reconcile this holistic notion of the group with the position that genocide must imply the physical destruction of the group?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, you know, when I argued the Krstic case ten years ago, Your Honours -- as a matter of fact, I believe you were on that panel ten years ago. I could be wrong, but I think that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And we did argue that it was necessary -- physical destruction was absolutely required and that displacement of the population could not be considered at all by the Trial Chamber and we lost on that. The court of appeal -- this Appeals Chamber said: No, that's just not so. Forcible transfer is an element, and that's where they talked about it in paragraphs 31 and 33 of the opinion, and then also obviously Judge Shahabuddeen. So that -- that notion has been rejected. So under current law, and obviously we accept that, you can have physical destruction even if -- on the theory, for example, that the community could not reconstitute itself. You know this -- the finding of the Krstic Appeals Chamber has been strongly criticised by commentators including Mr. Schabas in his article on genocide in the Florida Law Review, but we don't live in that academic world. So I'm accepting, I'm accepting fully the rationale and the holding, which we must, of course, as officers of this court, accepting the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement as absolutely binding precedent for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: Counsel, I just wanted to have some further clarification on this point. So if I understand correctly, there are three set of actions entailing genocide in this particular instance, meaning the killings, the forcible transfer, and destruction of homes, if I understand correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't think and I'll have check with my lead counsel here who has a superior knowledge of the facts -- yeah, no, we don't have the destruction of homes. That was in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: In the Krstic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Now, here we have the murders of the men and the forcible transfer, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: I just want to understand your submission. Do you mean to say that if we have proof of someone being involved in killings and if that same person has not been involved in another set of transactions that is part of the genocide, that person should be acquitted; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is. Because we read Krstic as requiring the combination of the killings and the forcible transfer because that's the only way you reach the conclusion that the genocidal intent was to destroy a part, the relevant part being the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. Killing of the men, again, it could be extermination, it could be murder; it's not genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: Let me put it another way, then. Let's just assume we are in a situation where the genocide only involved the killings, but there are many sets of killings, and here you have an accused being involved in specific sets of killings and not in some other sets of killings, would you say that still that person should be acquitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, it would depend, Your Honour, on the targeted group. We have to define what is the part. The Bosnian Muslims in this case, that was the ultimate group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The part of the group, as held by the Trial Chamber and as advanced by the Prosecution, was the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. So I'd have to know more in your hypothetical example of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: Yeah, so -- because that I put it -- I just base it on the facts that it seems here that the Trial Chamber did not say that forcible transfer did not exist, but maybe -- it was a fact of [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: A fact of -- I'm sorry. A fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: The forcible transfer -- the Trial Chamber did not say that it did not exist in this case. What the Trial Chamber says, based on what you are saying now, is that he was acquitted, he was not part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: But he was part of the killings, but still he should be acquitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIANG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm going to ask Mr. Gillett to comment on that particular point, your point that the targeted group from your understanding of Krstic must be the whole community, the Bosnian men and those who were forcibly transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think you addressed that point. You did point to parts of the judgement which substantiated the view that the killings themselves can provide genocidal intent. But would you like to comment on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, for the opportunity to address this question and my learned friend's submissions. As we read the Krstic appeal judgement - and I submit there is only one way to read it - at no point does it insert a requirement of proving forcible transfer or involvement therein in order to infer genocidal intent. At paragraph 27 it says very clearly, the last sentence of paragraph 27: "The killing of the military-aged men was, assuredly, a physical destruction, and given the scope of the killings the Trial Chamber could legitimately draw the inference that their extermination was motivated by genocidal intent." The fact of the forcible transfer was an additional consideration but not a necessary consideration. The targeted victims in this case were the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, and the Trial Chamber's finding that genocidal intent could be inferred from the killing of several thousand men and boys and the effects of those killings, the serious bodily and mental harm caused to the survivors and the families who have to live on in the shadow of these events, these are a basis from which you can infer genocidal intent and they're entirely in keeping with the Krstic appeal judgement. There is no requirement of proving forcible transfer in order to prove genocide. That's our submission, unless you have further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the submissions and the responses in respect of Mr. Beara. So we now move to the appeal of Drago Nikolic, and I call on counsel to present submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. President, Your Honours, I have the honour to address this honourable Appeals Chamber today and to begin the presentation of the oral arguments on behalf of Drago Nikolic. It is our submission that the Trial Chamber in this particular case committed both errors of law and factual errors which affected the judgement which entailed a conviction and strict sentences. We appeal to this Chamber to remedy the errors committed and we -- in our submission, the only appropriate outcome should be the acquittal of the appellant under some counts of the indictment and in a reduction of his sentence. Our oral arguments will be divided in six parts. The first part consists in our position that the sentence pronounced by the Trial Chamber is manifestly unlawful. Part two consists, in our submission, that the Trial Chamber erred by finding that Drago Nikolic -- finding that Drago Nikolic offered new uniforms to members of the 4th Battalion to persuade them to take part in the executions at Orahovac. I'm referring to grounds 13, 14, 20, and 26. Part three, the Trial Chamber erred by finding that Drago Nikolic ordered Slavko Peric, a member of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade to guard the prisoners at Kula school, knowing that they would be executed; these are grounds 23 and 24. Part four, the Trial Chamber erred by finding that Drago Nikolic called Sreten Acimovic, the commander of the 2nd Battalion, to pressurise him into executing the order that had come from above; these are grounds 15, 16, and 18 of Mr. Nikolic's appeal. Part five, the Trial Chamber erred by finding that Drago Nikolic was present at the execution site at Orahovac on the evening of the 14th of July, 1995; these are grounds 19, 22, and 25. And finally, part six, the Trial Chamber erred by finding that Drago Nikolic had knowledge that there was a massive killing operation being carried out with genocidal intent and that through his interaction with Beara and Popovic he was in a position to know of the genocidal intent. This covers grounds 4, 6, and 23 of Mr. Nikolic's appeal. Regarding the grounds of appeal 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, and 12, Mr. Nikolic stands by the arguments presented in his appeal brief and other submissions and will -- these will not be expanded upon today. Without any further delay, I will now give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Stephane Bourgon to continue the introduction. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, honourable Judges of the Appeals Chamber and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Before I begin my submissions this afternoon, Mr. President, I would like to say as a preliminary matter that yesterday I listened with great care to the arguments of my colleague from the Prosecution in response to Mr. Popovic's appeal. No doubt, Mr. President, the Prosecution was impressive in repeating the judgement in a narrative meant, of course, to impress the Appeals Chamber. But that's not my point. My point, Mr. President, this afternoon is that in its submissions yesterday, the Prosecution mentioned the name Drago Nikolic no less than 20 times in conjunction, of course, with the gentlemen called Beara and Popovic. Well, Mr. President, this is one of the most important issues in this case. Drago Nikolic was in no way close to Beara and Popovic during the events in July of 1995, nor was he close to them before that period, and he did not plan and co-ordinate the murder operation with them. At best, Drago Nikolic did meet with Beara and Popovic, from whom he received some instructions of a limited nature. This, Mr. President, is one of the main errors that was made by the Trial Chamber, as Drago Nikolic was tried, found guilty, and sentenced by association with the security branch, and this is definitely something that we wish to convince you otherwise during our arguments. Moving on to my introduction, Mr. President. Last week I attended the ADC Legacy Conference, during which Judge Moloto spoke, and he said one of the most important duties of the Defence counsel is to make the work of the Judges difficult. And I fully agree with him and I do intend to make your work difficult today by highlighting issues that go beneath the surface, that will force you to go and look deep into the evidence, and that will force you, Mr. President, to assess the manner in which the Trial Chamber committed numerous mistakes in this case. Well, it's tempting to say did the Trial Chamber get anything right? Well, it did. It did, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber did, on a macro level, get many things right. Today, as a result of the judgement, the victims know that men and combatants from the 12th Division of the ABiH, that is, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were in Srebrenica - I'm talking about those men and combatants who did not make it to the area of the 2nd Corps where they were all going - the victims know today that they were either killed in ambushes or they were made prisoners only to be executed in five different areas. That we know from the judgement. As a result of the judgement, the victims know the locations, they know where these people were executed, they know today about Orahovac and Lazete, the killing site. They know about Petkovci and Petkovci dam. They know about Kozluk and Rocevic. They also know about the cultural -- Pilica cultural centre as well as the Branjevo Farm. They know about these things. They even know about the reburial operation and the secondary mass graves, an absolute horror story. Well, in this regard, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber got many things right. However, and as we say in French: "C'est là que le bât blesse." Regarding the individual criminal responsibility of Drago Nikolic, with all due respect for the Trial Chamber, it was mistake after mistake after mistake. And this is the object of my arguments today because, Mr. President, the victims and their families in this case deserve better than the erroneous conclusions that were drawn on the basis of some witnesses who lied before this Court. If there's one thing that the Trial Chamber got right - and I'll come back to this - it is the fact that Drago Nikolic did not harbour genocidal intent. That's one of the findings I will also come back to. But immediately thereafter, the Trial Chamber erred by saying that he was aware of the genocidal intent of others and that he knew that this massive execution operation was conducted with genocidal intent. This is one of our grounds of appeal that we'll address at the end of my submissions. For the rest, Mr. President, it is important to look at how the Trial Chamber came to make such mistakes, such errors of law and errors of fact, but mostly errors of fact grounded on a wrong interpretation and assessment of the testimony of key witnesses. At this point I would like to move into closed session, Mr. President, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. President, you've seen before you the old lady, she's been looking at the Appeals Chamber and looking at us. In 2005, I started this case with this slide and I'm going to finish this case with the same slide. We invited the Trial Chamber then to look behind the obvious and obviously they did not. Now, I implore you, Mr. President, through our arguments as they will be presented today, we hope that you will see that the eye of the old is actually the ear, and that the nose is actually the chin, and that you will see the young lady, and you will see the truth and the merit to our arguments. I move to the first part of my argument, the manifestly excessive sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber. Why do we begin with the sentence? It's quite unusual. You don't see that very often, do you? Well, we do so simply because, first of all, in our brief we did it this way; but secondly and more importantly, because we wished to strongly emphasise the Trial Chamber's errors when imposing a sentence of 35 years' imprisonment on Drago Nikolic. This is a stand-alone ground, Mr. President, such that even if every other finding made by the Trial Chamber were to stand at the end of this appeal, we submit respectfully that the sentence must be lowered significantly. Our detailed arguments to that effect can be found in paragraphs 1 to 45 of our appellant's brief at ground number 1. Today I will focus on three issues. First of all, the errors in assessing the gravity of the crimes for which Mr. Nikolic was found guilty. Secondly, the impact of Drago Nikolic's personal character on the sentence, which led to other mistakes by the Trial Chamber. And the fact that the sentence imposed is a marked departure from sentences imposed on other accused in -- for the same crimes in similar circumstances. Moving on to the gravity, this will be addressed into three parts: The time-period, the Trial Chamber erred in identifying the time-period of Drago Nikolic's involvement; the Trial Chamber erred in the importance of the contribution of Drago Nikolic during the murder operation as well as his overall involvement in the Srebrenica events all together; and the Trial Chamber, lastly, the third point, in assessing the contribution of Drago Nikolic in comparison to others involved in the same events. First of all, in terms of the time-period, well, the Trial Chamber committed a mistake when it found that Drago Nikolic was involved in the JCE to murder from 13 July on the evening until 16 July in the afternoon. From a plain reading of the Trial Chamber's findings, the contribution of Drago Nikolic and his involvement in the murder operation ended on 15 July in the morning. It ended -- the last event was the alleged conversation he would have had with Acimovic, the commander of the 2nd Battalion, whom he would have called to put pressure on. We'll come back to this conversation which is actually one of our arguments during this appeal. But for now let's assume that the conversation took place. After this conversation, there is no longer any involvement of Drago Nikolic in the murder operation. Early in the morning he is on duty and he ends his shift or -- sorry, he doesn't end his shift, he begins his shift early in the morning on 15 July.
