For sure he begins his shift at 11.45, but according to the Trial Chamber he could have begun his shift as early as 0440. There is no finding from the Trial Chamber that he had any involvement in Rocevic during the period from the 15th of July until the 16th. This is at judgement 1372. The Trial Chamber found that Nikolic was not at Rocevic, 1370; and the Trial Chamber found that the last entry in the log written by Drago Nikolic on the 16th of July was not linked to the JCE. The Prosecution tried to say that this entry in the log-book - and that is P377 at pages 148-149 - the Prosecution argued that this entry meant that he was sending ammunition for the killings probably in Branjevo Farm or Pilica cultural centre, and the Trial Chamber found that this was not the case. In the morning of 16 July he ended his shift. He is at Standard barracks, the headquarters, the command of the brigade, but we don't know what he's doing. What we know is that a little later he will go and have lunch with his wife because it's her birthday. By the way, the Trial Chamber missed that all together and this is in the statement of Vida Vasic, 3D474, and also in the transcript at 25935. And thereafter Drago Nikolic took part in the preparations for the funeral of his cousin, and he took part in the funeral ceremonies the next day, thereby completely extracting himself from the murder operation. But right in the morning, in the morning of 16 July, when he finishes his shift and he is replaced, and the evidence shows that he was replaced that morning by another duty officer, he's at the brigade and he is not involved. We all know what's happening during this time-frame at the Kula school, the Branjevo Farm, and later in the afternoon at the Pilica cultural centre. He's just not there. And these are based on the findings of the Trial Chamber. Second point is what about the overall contribution of Drago Nikolic in the Srebrenica events and during the murder operation? What did he do exactly? We'll begin with the Srebrenica events. The Srebrenica events, I mean this case is not just about what happened in Zvornik, it started before that. It started as a minimum with the launching of the Krivaja 95, an operation that was planned months before, 2 July a preparation order. Then brigades send troops as part of the battle that is about to take place to capture Srebrenica. Then we capture Srebrenica. And then we separate the men from their families. And then we do the forcible transfer of the women, the children, and the elderly. And then we make the members of the column prisoners. And then the executions begin at Cerska Valley. And then more executions at the Kravica warehouse, thousands of people. And then the transport of the prisoners are taken to Bratunac. My colleague in his last argument went out of his way to explain how a security risk the presence of the prisoners in Bratunac was and how at some point it was decided to take some of them to the Zvornik area. And then we have the executions, five places: Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, Branjevo Military Farm, Pilica cultural centre. And then we sweep the area to ensure that any Muslims left behind will be killed. And then we got the Branjevo Farm survivors who disappear. And then we got the Milici hospital prisoners who disappear. And then we do this reburial operation. This, at a minimum, and I cut short here is Srebrenica. Where is Drago Nikolic in all of that? Well, here is where Drago Nikolic is: He's there when he receives a phone call on the 13th of July, a phone call that we are challenging. He's present at the school in Orahovac, there's no point in denying this. Drago Nikolic said it himself when he spoke to the Trial Chamber at the end of the trial. He was present at some point in the day at Orahovac school. And then of course he was involved - I put a circle around Kozluk and Rocevic because of those conversations that we are challenging. Other than that, this is Drago Nikolic. We say the Trial Chamber erred in failing to see this. What about his contribution during those -- that period? We already said that it's limited from the 13th to the 15th. Well, during the 13th to the 15th, what he did during the 13th to the 15th, a junior officer, drawn into specific aspects of an ongoing overwhelming operation that he possessed limited knowledge of, that of a junior officer having no influence whatsoever executing the orders issued by the chain of command through his superiors and sometimes to those who are not even his superiors, that of a junior officer who succeeded in extracting himself from this nightmare. We say that the Trial Chamber erred in not seeing the real contribution of Drago Nikolic to this operation. For the rest, of course, we know that we are challenging his presence at Orahovac at the killing site. We are challenging the thing about the uniform. And we are challenging the conversations with Acimovic. In terms of the gravity, of course, there is also the relative contribution of Drago Nikolic in comparison with others. I will just use two examples, the first one is Borovcanin and the second one is Pandurevic. Borovcanin, deputy commander of the special police brigade of the MUP, involved and present in the separation of men from their families, connected to the executions at the Kravica warehouse. According to the Trial Chamber, he saw at least one busload of dead bodies on the site. His acts in ordering his men to participate, according to the Trial Chamber, constituted a substantial contribution to the crime of forcible transfer. He's involved in the operations to block the column and he had the authority and ability to influence these events. And as we know, on the 15th of July, at midday, he meets with Dragan Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, to talk about the upcoming operations to try and block the column. He is much more involved than Drago Nikolic, and that the Trial Chamber did not take into account, Mr. President. Pandurevic, the brigade commander, involved in the attack and capture of Srebrenica, involved in the situation in Zepa. He has direct access to Mladic. He has direct access to Krstic. He's involved in fighting the column and in preventing the Bosnian Muslims from reaching the 2nd Corps of the ABiH territory. Now, as of 15 July in the morning, the Trial Chamber found that this man learned what was going on in his territory. He knows that thousands of people are located in the Zvornik area to be killed. And then the story goes on, and I'm not going to get involved in Pandurevic's story, that's not my case. Then of course he's involved in the killing of the patients on the Milici hospital, the same people who while they were in the custody of Drago Nikolic were kept safe, that's a finding from the Trial Chamber. And most of all is the fact that the brigade commander, if someone had the authority, the capability, the ability, and the guts to do this and to stop this from taking place, it was the brigade commander. When we look at the contribution of Drago Nikolic and the contribution of others, this must be assessed, Mr. President, and the Trial Chamber, in our view, failed to do so. I see I have five minutes, I go on to my next point in terms of the impact of Drago Nikolic's personal character. I'll try to speed up a bit so I can finish this ground tonight. In terms of his character, well, we know that Drago Nikolic is a second lieutenant, again I started with this in this case in 2005 and I'll say it again, the lowest possible rank in the military scale as compared to all those generals that have been charged and found guilty. In terms of the character of Drago Nikolic, we have especially the fact that he was not a graduate from the military academy, the fact that nobody liked him or trusted him because he was not a real "officer." The fact that because he was the chief of security and had to investigate on his buddies that nobody liked him because nobody likes the security, that's just part of the game when you have to investigate your colleagues. The fact that the commander of the brigade, Pandurevic, described Drago Nikolic as wearing a coat too big for him. He said the security coat was much too big for him. And then Drago Nikolic, lastly, was perturbed, to say the least, about what he was asked to do, even if it was less than what the Trial Chamber thinks he was asked to do. When he comes out of that meeting with Beara and Popovic on the 14th of July in the morning, he speaks to his driver, Bircakovic, and he tells Bircakovic -- Bircakovic testifies, he says he was mad, he couldn't believe what he was being asked to do for all those people coming in for an exchange. Why not believe Bircakovic that this is what Drago Nikolic said? Bircakovic was used, his testimony was used, in many other areas where the Trial Chamber relied on Bircakovic's testimony. But for this, no, he didn't say that because that would not be too convenient. Of course, there's a link with the conversation the night before which we will come back to. Mr. President, I will stop here for today because I see the time is running by. I just have one small argument to do tomorrow morning to finish with this ground and that is simply the fact that this sentence, 35 years' imprisonment, even if everything else is true and stands after this appeal, is a marked departure from sentences imposed on others. And the two examples I will use tomorrow is Krstic, the big general at the top of the operation, convicted of aiding and abetting for 35 -- and sentenced to 35 years, and Jokic, someone who's still higher than Drago Nikolic but lower in the food chain and who also involved in sending engineering equipment to the killing sites and he's also a duty officer at the brigade, and I will also come back on this, and he got nine years. So 35 years is a marked departure which is motived by only one thing and it's simply because he was a security officer. That ends my submissions for today, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we do, may I just raise a housekeeping question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Just conscious of the order of things tomorrow, I anticipate that we will conclude Mr. Bourgon's client's case tomorrow morning, which will take us to Pandurevic. And it is possible, I think, having spoken with Mr. Haynes, that we may get through that tomorrow afternoon. My question for Your Honours is whether you would intend to start the Prosecution's appeal before you had completed the Defence appeals from Mr. Miletic. I would presume Your Honours would not intend doing that, but I wondered if I might just clarify that with you now. It will assist us greatly if Your Honours could confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we wouldn't do that. We will finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, I didn't think you would. I just wanted to check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so we're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
